shiftMode: Call for help early — assign roles: airway, meds, monitor, suction, backup airway, post-intubation sedation.
Preoxygenate aggressively; consider nasal cannula, NRB, NIV, or BVM with PEEP.
Have suction immediately reachable before the first attempt.
Choose first-pass and backup plans before pushing meds — video/direct laryngoscopy, boujee, supraglottic, cricothyrotomy.
Name plan and action before performing so team is aware.
Maximum 3+1 attempts: three, plus one final attempt by a more experienced colleague only. Change something material each attempt.
Physiology kills before anatomy: optimize hypotension, hypoxemia, severe acidosis, RV failure, and hyperkalemia when possible.
Confirm with continuous waveform capnography.
Give post-intubation analgesia and sedation, and reassess the ventilator.
indications: Failure to oxygenate or ventilate
Inability to protect airway
Expected clinical deterioration requiring airway control
Severe agitation or injury requiring controlled oxygenation/ventilation
Cardiac arrest or peri-arrest airway management when appropriate
contraindications: Anticipated impossible oral intubation should trigger alternate plan early
Severe physiologic instability may require resuscitation before induction when time allows
Suspected cervical spine injury: not a contraindication to intubation or to paralysis. See positioning.
anatomy: Align oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes when using direct laryngoscopy; ear-to-sternal-notch positioning is ideal.
Identify epiglottis, arytenoids, posterior cartilages, and cords.
In obesity or pregnancy, ramp aggressively rather than placing the patient flat.
equipment: Monitor: cardiac monitor, pulse ox, BP cycling, waveform capnography ready
Preoxygenation setup: NRB, nasal cannula, BVM with PEEP, NIV as needed
Suction connected and tested
Video laryngoscope and/or direct laryngoscope with working light
ET tubes: planned size plus one size smaller
Stylet and bougie
10 mL syringe for cuff inflation and a cuff manometer
ETCO2 detector / continuous waveform capnography
Tube holder or tape
Backup supraglottic airway
Cricothyrotomy kit available for high-risk airway
Induction and paralytic medications drawn up and labeled
Post-intubation analgesia/sedation ordered or ready
positioning: Place patient ear-to-sternal-notch when possible.
Ramped position for obesity, pregnancy, or poor neck mobility.
Head elevated when tolerated to prolong safe apnea time.
Suspected cervical spine injury: minimize movement rather than immobilize rigidly. Manual in-line stabilization, jaw thrust rather than head tilt and chin lift, and videolaryngoscopy where available.
Remove the front of the collar for laryngoscopy and have the assistant hold the head.
steps: Assess airway difficulty and physiologic risk.
Preoxygenate and optimize hemodynamics before induction when possible.
Verbalize primary and backup airway plan.
Prepare equipment, suction, capnography, tube securement, and post-intubation medications.
Administer induction and paralytic medications when ready.
Perform laryngoscopy with deliberate epiglottis and glottic identification.

Pass the tube under continuous direct or video visualization. With a hyperangulated videolaryngoscope blade use a stylet, bougie, or flexible bronchoscope. Do not advance a bougie blind at a Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 view.

Between attempts, change something informed by the last one: position, laryngoscope or blade, introducer, operator, external laryngeal manipulation, suction, removal of cricoid force, or optimized neuromuscular block.
After 3+1 unsuccessful attempts declare 'failed intubation', move to Plan B, summon assistance, and decide to do surgical airway.
Inflate the cuff to the minimum that stops the leak and measure it: 20-30 cmH2O.
Confirm continuous waveform capnography and bilateral chest rise; check for right mainstem.

Secure the tube at a documented depth - about 21 cm at the incisors in women and 23 cm in men, or three times the tube size - then obtain a chest x-ray when appropriate and reassess ventilator and sedation.
confirmation: Two-point check: the tube seen passing through the vocal cords AND sustained exhaled carbon dioxide on waveform capnography. Sustained capnography excludes esophageal placement but cannot by itself exclude bronchial or pharyngeal position.
Bilateral chest rise and breath sounds
Absent gastric insufflation sounds
Appropriate oxygenation/ventilation response
Chest x-ray for depth and complications when clinically appropriate
troubleshooting: Hypoxemia: abandon the attempt, prioritize facemask oxygenation. Oxygenate between attempts; maintain anesthesia.
Poor view: optimize position, suction, external laryngeal manipulation, change blade or laryngoscope, optimize neuromuscular block. Do not insert a bougie blind at a grade 3-4 view.
Cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate: supraglottic airway or surgical airway pathway immediately.
Sugammadex reliance: it does not rescue a cannot-intubate cannot-oxygenate patient now. 16 mg/kg reverses rocuronium in about three minutes - oxygenate and go to the front of the neck.
Post-intubation hypotension: check tube depth, breath stacking/auto-PEEP, tension pneumothorax, sedation effect, occult shock; start fluids/pressors as appropriate.
High peak pressures: consider bronchospasm, tube obstruction, mainstem, pneumothorax, or ventilator mismatch.
complications: Failed airway requiring supraglottic or surgical airway
aftercare: Start analgesia and sedation immediately unless deliberately held for neurological assessment; if held, say so out loud to the team.
Set ventilator based on disease state; reassess plateau pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, and hemodynamics.
Obtain chest x-ray when appropriate to confirm depth and evaluate complications.
Reassess tube depth after transport or major position changes.
documentation: Indication for intubation: airway protection, respiratory failure, or anticipated clinical deterioration.
Consent when feasible; emergency justification when delay would risk patient harm.
Preoxygenation and monitoring: cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, capnography.
Medications, as documented in MAR.
Tube placement under visualization and secured depth.
Devices used: laryngoscope and blade type, tube size, introducer, and any adjunct.
Number of attempts, what was changed between them, and the view obtained.
Difficulty encountered and how it was resolved. Difficult airway: verbal handover to the ongoing team plus a chart record, not the procedure note alone.
Confirmation: continuous waveform capnography and clinical assessment.
Tolerance of procedure; complications documented separately.
seniorPearls: Your first attempt should be your best attempt. Do not burn an attempt while still setting up.
If the patient is crashing from physiology, a beautiful view of the cords will not save them by itself.
Have the post-intubation plan ready before induction.

medicationDosing.indication: Rapid sequence induction and intubation, adult. Doses are targets, not ceilings.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Give an induction agent with the paralytic - never a paralytic alone. Choose the agent by physiology, not habit; see agent of choice below. In shock the two move in opposite directions: halve the induction dose and give the full paralytic dose, because a slow circulation delays onset and an underdosed paralytic leaves you a straining patient.

medications.caution: For raised ICP, pain, or tachycardia. Will drop the blood pressure in a patient who is already compensating: omit it or halve it in shock.
No analgesia. Brief myoclonus. Cortisol suppression may carry a negative prognostic implication in sepsis. Halve the dose in shock.

May induce cardiac ischemia or arrhythmias, and increases salivation. Use in raised intracranial pressure remains controversial. Not hemodynamically neutral in a catecholamine-depleted patient - the direct myocardial depression is unmasked once the sympathetic reserve is gone, so halve the dose in shock.
Hypotension, bradycardia, negative inotropy, and 2-5 minutes to peak. A last resort for induction when nothing else is available, not an equal alternative to the agents above.
Potent vasodilation and significant hypotension. Contraindicated with egg or soybean allergy. Dose on lean body weight, and halve it in shock.

DAS 2025 specifies 1.2 mg/kg for RSI; the lower end of this range gives slower onset and may not give RSI-grade conditions. Dose on ideal body weight. Outlasts a single induction dose by about 35 minutes - sedation afterwards is not optional.
Hyperkalemia risk. Avoid in malignant hyperthermia, neuromuscular disease, rhabdomyolysis, and stroke or burns more than 72 h old. Dose on total body weight.

medicationDosing.sourceNote: Doses from tl;dr pharmacy, 'The Pharmacist's Do's and Don'ts of Rapid Sequence Intubation' (2023), accepted by the clinical owner and re-affirmed unchanged on 2026-07-30. That source cites no primary references. Intravenous lidocaine and defasciculating vecuronium were removed from pretreatment on 2026-07-30: neither is supported by current evidence. Paediatric atropine is omitted because this record is adult-scoped.
selectionGuidance: Status epilepticus: etomidate, propofol, or midazolam.
Hemodynamic instability or distributive shock: etomidate or ketamine.
Severe bronchospasm: etomidate, ketamine, or propofol.

shiftMode: Confirm indication, site, side, anticoagulation/coagulopathy status.
Full sterile barrier: cap, mask, gown, gloves, wide chlorhexidine prep, large drape.
Ultrasound before puncture: identify vein, artery, thrombus, depth, compressibility, and safest trajectory.
Never dilate until Ultrasound confirms the wire in two planes, or transduce, every time — no emergency exception.
Keep control of the wire at all times.
Confirm placement and screen for complications per site and institutional practice.
indications: Vasopressor or irritant medication administration
Poor peripheral access with need for reliable central access
Central venous pressure monitoring
Massive transfusion or high-flow resuscitation when appropriate catheter chosen
Temporary access while definitive access is arranged
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection or burn over intended insertion site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at intended site
Uncorrected coagulopathy (relative)
anatomy: IJ: vein is commonly lateral/anterior to carotid but anatomy varies.
Femoral: NAVEL lateral-to-medial reminder is imperfect.
Subclavian/axillary access has pneumothorax and noncompressible bleeding considerations.
Always distinguish compressible vein from pulsatile/noncompressible artery before puncture.
equipment: Central line kit with catheter, wire, needle, scalpel, dilator, and caps
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape, chlorhexidine scrub
Ultrasound machine
Sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Flushes for all ports
Suture or securement device
Biopatch or antimicrobial dressing
Transparent sterile dressing
Sharps container and sterile towels
Chest x-ray or confirmation
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, avoid excessive rotation.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Place the ultrasound screen in your line of sight before sterile prep.
steps: Confirm indication and choose site based on urgency, anatomy, infection risk, bleeding risk, and clinical need.
Perform ultrasound survey before opening the kit.
Prep and drape using full sterile barrier technique.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along planned tract.
Cannulate vein under ultrasound guidance, maintaining needle tip awareness.
Pass the guidewire smoothly without force, keeping a hand on it at all times.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating: ultrasound in short and long axis planes. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce or manometer before dilating.
Make small skin nick while controlling wire.
Dilate over wire without force; stop if resistance or uncertainty.
Advance catheter over wire, remove wire while maintaining catheter control, and state aloud that the wire is out and intact while looking at it.
Occlude every hub the moment the wire is out - cap, clamp, or connected tubing - so the catheter is never open to air.
Aspirate and flush all ports.
Secure catheter and apply sterile dressing.
Confirm position.
ultrasound: Use short-axis for vessel identification; consider long-axis for needle tip tracking if skilled.
Compress vein before sterile prep to evaluate patency and thrombus.
Confirm the guidewire in the vein in two planes before dilation - short axis to exclude the artery, long axis to show it tracking centrally.
confirmation: All ports aspirate and flush easily
Guidewire removed intact and confirmed aloud
Catheter secured with sterile dressing
Appropriate imaging/confirmation obtained based on site
Tip at the SVC/right atrial junction on chest x-ray, at or just above the carina
A normal chest x-ray does not exclude arterial placement; transduce the catheter if there is any doubt
No immediate evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; check needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Color, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not answer it.

Arterial puncture with the needle only (18 G or smaller, not dilated): withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. After a neck puncture watch the airway for several hours - a carotid hematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it and do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and call vascular surgery and interventional radiology now. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, hemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Resistance with dilator: stop; confirm wire path and vessel location before proceeding.
No blood return from one port: check clamp/cap, flush gently, reposition; do not force against resistance.

Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub: suspect air embolism - occlude the hub, left lateral decubitus head-down, 100% oxygen, and aspirate from a central lumen if one is in place.
Unstable after line: consider pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or unrelated shock progression.
complications: Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian/axillary approaches
aftercare: Label line and date dressing per local policy.
Review imaging/confirmation before using for high-risk infusions if required by site/policy.
Remove unnecessary lines as soon as clinically appropriate.
Reassess insertion site for bleeding or hematoma after placement.
documentation: Indication for central venous catheter.
Consent, or emergent need if consent not possible.
Site and side; full sterile barrier precautions.
Ultrasound guidance for vessel identification and cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance, removed intact.
All ports aspirated and flushed; catheter secured with sterile dressing.
Placement confirmation and immediate complication assessment.
seniorPearls: The catastrophic errors come after venous puncture, not before: wire control, dilation, confirmation.
If the wire does not pass smoothly, the answer is never more force.
Open the exact catheter you need. A triple lumen is not a Cordis and not a dialysis catheter.
After two failed passes, change something: the site, the operator, or the plan.
If a large-bore device ends up in an artery, leave it in and make the call.

shiftMode: Document pre-block neurovascular status.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Small volume; aspirate before each increment; inject slowly, in stages.
Allow onset time; reassess anesthesia and distal perfusion before the procedure.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Laceration repair
Nailbed injury
Foreign body removal
Paronychia or minor drainage procedure
Fracture or dislocation analgesia adjunct
contraindications: Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Allergy to planned anesthetic
Infection over the injection site, or over the path where an alternate approach is available
Major vascular compromise - do not delay urgent surgical evaluation
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy (relative)
anatomy: Digital nerves run along the medial and lateral aspects of the digit with their vessels.
Injection at the base can reach dorsal and volar branches, depending on technique.
Avoid circumferential high-volume injection - unnecessary tissue pressure.
equipment: 1% lidocaine without epinephrine for a short block, or 0.25% bupivacaine when the repair needs hours. Epinephrine in a digit is safer than traditionally taught; follow local policy.
3-5 mL syringe
25-30G needle
Chlorhexidine-alcohol prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; sterile probe cover and gel if using ultrasound
Gauze and dressing supplies
Tray for the repair or drainage
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you inject.
positioning: Hand or foot on a stable surface.
Expose the whole digit; remove rings before swelling worsens.
Keep the patient from watching if that increases anxiety.
steps: Confirm digit, injury, and neurovascular status.
Clean the injection site.
Insert at the base of the digit, dorsolateral, per technique.
Aspirate before injection.
Inject slowly while withdrawing or redirecting.
Repeat on the opposite side if needed.
Wait several minutes; test anesthesia.
Proceed once anesthesia is adequate.
confirmation: Improved pain or numbness in the target distribution
Distal perfusion intact
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Test the target territory before blocking: light touch or cold, and motor function where present, against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Severe pain with injection: slow down, reposition, buffer or warm the anesthetic.
Poor perfusion after injection: remove constrictive dressing or rings, reassess volume and epinephrine, escalate if persistent.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
Nerve irritation or injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity, rare at digital block volumes - see the linked rescue card
aftercare: Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Wound-specific aftercare.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Digital nerve block for analgesia of the affected digit.
Verbal consent and site confirmation.
Skin prep; clean/sterile technique.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
No immediate complications.

agents.note: Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. Lower risk of severe cardiotoxicity than bupivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting - do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: This procedure is when you cannot oxygenate or ventilate your patient.
Call failed airway out loud; assign someone to keep oxygenating while you prep the neck.
Continue passive oxygenation from above throughout procedure, including once cutting starts — leave the facemask or supraglottic device in place and keep delivering.
Ensure full neuromuscular block before you cut — even apneic, a straining patient or closed glottis makes the procedure harder and oxygenation worse.
Landmark before the airway is lost if the airway looks high risk.
Prep wide if time allows — don't let sterile technique delay oxygenation in a true cannot-oxygenate crisis.

One technique: scalpel-bougie-tube (DAS 2025) — number 10 blade, bougie, 6.0 cuffed tracheal tube. A commercial Seldinger kit is a different procedure; if that's what's stocked, follow its instructions instead.
Confirm with ETCO2 and chest rise; secure aggressively.
indications: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate after failed tracheal intubation, supraglottic rescue, and facemask oxygenation.
Failed airway with rapidly worsening hypoxemia
Upper airway obstruction where oral/nasal approach is not feasible
Massive facial trauma or airway contamination when standard approaches fail
contraindications: This technique indicated only for Adult. Pediatric patients < 8-10 years require cannula-based approach due to different anatomy —cricothyroid membrane is small, high, and soft.
Laryngeal fracture or distorted neck anatomy may make landmarks unreliable
Coagulopathy (relative)
anatomy: Cricothyroid membrane lies between thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage.
Stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand.
In obesity or edema, make a generous vertical skin incision first to find the membrane.
equipment: Number 10 scalpel blade, not a pointed 11 or 15 - risk of repeated stabs and posterior wall injury.
Bougie
6.0 cuffed tracheal tube.
Tracheal hook or dilator if available
Suction
BVM with oxygen
Capnography
Securing device/tape
Commercial cricothyrotomy kit
positioning: Supine when possible
Extend the neck fully unless contraindicated; neutral with manual in-line stabilization if cervical spine injury is a concern
Stand at head or side based on access
Expose neck widely
steps: Identify and stabilize the larynx with the non-dominant hand, and do not let go until the tube is in.
Palpable membrane: transverse stab incision straight through it. Otherwise make an 8-10 cm vertical midline skin incision first, dissect bluntly with a finger down to the larynx, then stab.
Keep the scalpel in the hole and rotate the blade 90 degrees so the sharp edge points towards the feet. It is now the guide for the bougie.
Slide the bougie along the blade, angled towards the feet, into the trachea. Advance 10-15 cm and no further; deeper risks the carina and the posterior tracheal wall.
Remove the scalpel and railroad the 6.0 cuffed tube over the bougie with a gentle twist.
Advance only until the cuff has passed the membrane, then about 1-2 cm more. A 6.0 tube pushed to its usual 21 cm mark sits in the right main bronchus.
Remove the bougie, inflate the cuff, ventilate, and confirm ETCO2 and chest rise.
Secure the tube and reassess oxygenation and ventilation.
ultrasound: Assess membrane palpability before induction whenever a difficult airway is anticipated, and if it is impalpable, locate and mark the membrane with ultrasound before you start.
Do not scan during an established cannot-oxygenate crisis.
confirmation: Continuous waveform ETCO2
Capnography can be flat in a correctly sited tube when cardiac output is very low or the patient has been hypoxic long enough to arrest.
Bilateral chest rise
Improving oxygen saturation if circulation intact
Ability to ventilate without massive leak
Condensation in tube
Chest x-ray after stabilization
troubleshooting: Cannot find membrane: typical for obesity, edema, or neck hematoma - make an 8-10 cm vertical midline skin incision first, dissect bluntly with a finger down to the larynx, then stab.
Lost the tract: do not hunt with the bougie. Re-stabilize the larynx, extend the skin incision vertically, and find the hole again with a finger.
Tube will not pass: rotate, use smaller tube, confirm bougie is intratracheal.
No ETCO2: reassess placement, obstruction, circuit, and circulation.
Bleeding: suction aggressively; oxygenation remains priority.
aftercare: Secure it well; accidental dislodgement loses the airway.
Once stabilized, exclude bronchial intubation and pneumothorax: chest rise, breath sounds, tube depth, and chest x-ray.
Arrange early surgical or ENT review and a definitive airway plan.
Document failed airway context and rescue rationale.
documentation: Emergent cricothyrotomy for failed airway / cannot intubate-cannot oxygenate.
Emergency justification: immediate threat to life, delay would risk patient harm.

shiftMode: For tamponade physiology in context, not an effusion alone.
Ultrasound picks pocket and path. Subxiphoid landmark route: fallback when there is no machine.
Aortic dissection or post-infarction free-wall rupture: surgical, not needle — see contraindications.
Resuscitation, pressors, blood, and surgical backup moving in parallel when indicated.
Advance under visualization if possible; aspirate continuously or frequently.
20-50 mL often reverses tamponade; you may stop there.
Tamponade can coexist with bleeding, tension pneumothorax, or profound hypovolemia.
indications: Cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise
Peri-arrest/arrest with ultrasound evidence of tamponade
Diagnostic/therapeutic drainage when benefits outweigh risks
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening tamponade, except the two below.
Aortic dissection with hemopericardium: surgical emergency, not a needle. Restoring pressure raises the gradient across the tear, converting a contained rupture into an uncontained one.
Post-infarction free-wall rupture: same mechanism. Cardiothoracic surgery now.

Narrow exception for both (ESC): impending arrest, no immediate surgical option. Drain small aliquots, about 10-20 mL at a time, to the lowest blood pressure that perfuses rather than a normal one; stop there. Aliquot size is local.
Purulent effusion or organized clot: needle and pigtail clear neither - surgical drainage.
Coagulopathy: caution, may be outweighed by shock.
Adult scope; pediatric needle length, drainage volume, and sedation differ.
anatomy: Subxiphoid, parasternal, or apical: largest pocket with the shortest safe path.
Parasternal: the internal mammary artery runs close and parallel to the sternal edge. Find it on color Doppler; do not trust a distance in centimeters.
Parasternal and apical: enter just above the superior border of the rib below the target space; intercostal vessels and nerve run along the inferior margin of the rib above.
Subxiphoid: longest path, closest to the liver. Blind fallback: 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, about 30-45 degrees to the skin, aimed at the left shoulder.
Target the fluid pocket; steer away from the myocardium.
equipment: Ultrasound with sterile cover, gel, and color Doppler

steps: Confirm effusion with tamponade physiology or instability; exclude dissection and free-wall rupture.
Pick the largest pocket with the shortest safe path; mark the site and read the depth off the screen.
Prep/drape and anesthetize if time allows.
Advance under real-time visualization, aspirating, watching the tip rather than the hub.
Emergency phase: aspirate only until perfusion returns, commonly 20-50 mL. Then stop, re-scan, and decide on a catheter. Do not continue because fluid keeps coming.
Before dilating over the wire, see the wire inside the pericardial space - no exception, including in an emergency.
Place the catheter by Seldinger; confirm the catheter itself, not just the wire, in the pericardial space.
Secure, attach closed drainage, reassess with ultrasound and hemodynamics.
After stabilization, stage drainage: initial total under about 500 mL, then at intervals, not continuously. Rapid large-volume removal causes pericardial decompression syndrome.
ultrasound: In-plane when skill and window allow.

Tip in pericardium or chamber uncertain: inject a few milliliters of agitated saline. Bubbles in the pericardial space confirm position; bubbles in a cardiac chamber mean you are inside the heart - do not dilate.
Re-scan after drainage: residual fluid and cardiac filling.
confirmation: Improved blood pressure/perfusion
Improved tachycardia or arrest physiology
Ultrasound decrease in effusion and resolution of tamponade findings
Confirm position with agitated saline, direct view of the catheter in the space, or a transduced waveform: a ventricular pressure trace means the catheter is in the ventricle.
Hemopericardium: the aspirate is blood, so its color proves nothing.
Pericardial blood usually does not clot in the syringe; brisk clotting suggests intracardiac blood. Supporting sign only, not confirmation.
troubleshooting: No aspirate: reassess window, needle depth, clot, or wrong diagnosis.

Bright pulsatile or briskly clotting blood: stop, do not dilate, confirm position. Needle intracardiac: withdraw and watch - a needle hole usually seals - then re-scan for a new or enlarging effusion.
Fluid returns, nothing improves: clot, a second loculated pocket, or not tamponade. Clot needs surgery.
Collapse after apparently successful drainage: pericardial decompression syndrome. Stop draining; fluid and inotropy; echo and cardiology.
Recurrent instability: re-scan for reaccumulation, clot, tension pneumothorax, hemorrhage, or another obstructive cause.
complications: Right ventricular laceration from dilating or railroading a catheter over a misplaced wire
Internal mammary or intercostal artery injury
Pericardial decompression syndrome: paradoxical collapse, pulmonary edema, or ventricular dysfunction after drainage, typically after rapid or large-volume removal
aftercare: Continuous monitoring and repeat ultrasound.
Watch for decompression syndrome for hours after a large drainage, including on the ward.

Staged drainage, output recorded. Cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery sets the removal target; commonly output below roughly 25-30 mL/day with no significant reaccumulation on echo. Exact figure is local.
Send fluid by etiology before discarding: cell count, culture including mycobacteria, cytology, protein/LDH as indicated.

visualAssets.title: Ultrasound target confirmation
visualAssets.subtitle: Subxiphoid view showing pericardial effusion, myocardium, drainage target, and needle tip entering the fluid pocket.

visualAssets.title: Subxiphoid needle geometry (no-ultrasound fallback)
visualAssets.subtitle: Blind fallback route only, for when no machine is available. Needle enters 1 cm below the costal margin just left of the xiphoid, tracks shallowly under the costal margin at about 30-45 degrees, and aims toward the left shoulder.
visualAssets.caption: Blind fallback: enter 1 cm below the left costal margin beside the xiphoid and aim at the left shoulder; inset: shallow under the costal margin at 30-45 degrees into the effusion.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Use when unstable bradycardia is not responding or needs bridge therapy.
Keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors running while placing, if unstable.
Know the generator before you need it — rate, output in mA, sensitivity, battery, and which cable mates it to this catheter.
Electrical capture is not enough — confirm mechanical capture with pulse/BP/arterial waveform.
Spikes with no capture at maximum output means malposition, not a generator problem — reposition rather than increasing output.
Secure catheter and generator carefully; dislodgement is common.
Do not remove backup pads or pressors until capture is reliable and the catheter is secured.
indications: Unstable bradycardia refractory to medications/transcutaneous pacing
High-grade AV block with instability
Reversible bradycardia - drug toxicity, hyperkalemia, Lyme carditis, myocarditis - where pacing bridges to resolution
Bridge to permanent pacing or definitive management
contraindications: No absolute contraindication in life-threatening bradycardia
Prosthetic tricuspid valve - a pacing lead cannot be floated across a mechanical tricuspid
Severe agitation may require sedation/airway planning
Infection or thrombus at access site affects site selection
Adult scope.
anatomy: Right internal jugular is the preferred route.
Left subclavian is the second choice for a longer dwell. Avoid an intrathoracic subclavian puncture - it risks pneumothorax and it compromises the vein a permanent device may need.
Femoral works and is sometimes the only option, but it carries higher infection and thrombosis rates and loses capture with leg movement.
Preserve the side planned for the permanent pacemaker.
The balloon-tipped catheter floats with blood flow toward the RV when advanced correctly. From the right internal jugular the right ventricle is typically at about 30-35 cm.
ECG changes and capture help guide placement.
equipment: Central venous introducer sized to this pacing catheter
Balloon-tipped pacing catheter with its sterile contamination sleeve and locking mechanism
Pacing generator with battery checked, and the specific connector cable that mates it to this catheter
A syringe of air for the balloon - air only, never fluid or contrast
Sterile setup
Monitor/defib pads
Ultrasound for venous access
Flushes
Suture/securement
Pressors and transcutaneous pacing available
positioning: Supine
Sterile central line position based on chosen access site
Defib pads on patient
steps: Obtain central venous access and place the introducer.
Test the balloon before it goes in, then connect the pacing catheter to the generator and confirm it paces.
Set the generator before insertion: rate about 60-80 or above the patient's own rate, output high to start at around 5-10 mA, and the mode the rhythm calls for.
Inflate the balloon, typically 1.0-1.5 mL of air.
Advance gently while watching the ECG for ectopy and capture. Never advance against resistance, and never advance or withdraw with the balloon inflated against resistance.
Capture, then find the threshold: reduce the output until capture is lost, note that number, and set the output at two to three times it.
Confirm mechanical capture with pulse, blood pressure, or arterial waveform.
Deflate the balloon, secure the catheter and the generator, and obtain a chest radiograph for position, depth, and pneumothorax.
Record rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth.
ultrasound: Ultrasound helps obtain venous access and may help assess catheter course/complications.
confirmation: Electrical capture on ECG
Mechanical capture with palpable pulse/BP/arterial waveform
Improved perfusion/mental status
Chest x-ray for catheter position, depth, and complications
troubleshooting: No capture at maximum output: position, not power. Deflate, withdraw a few centimeters, reinflate, and refloat. Keep transcutaneous pacing and pressors going while you do.
Intermittent capture: secure, reposition, increase output margin.
Threshold rising over hours: the catheter is migrating or the tip is becoming inflamed. Recheck position and securement, and hand that number over to the next team.
Ventricular ectopy: withdraw/reposition if irritating myocardium.
Sudden hypotension after a good capture: think right ventricular perforation and tamponade. Scan.
Hypotension despite capture: reassess rate, shock, medications, and mechanical complications.
Diaphragmatic pacing or hiccups: the tip is against the diaphragmatic surface or through the wall. Reassess position.
complications: Bleeding or hematoma at the access site
aftercare: Continuous monitoring.
Cardiology/ICU admission
Review the need every day and document the plan. Dwell time drives infection, thrombosis, and displacement
Repeat capture checks after movement/transport.
Keep transcutaneous pacing capability and pressors immediately available for the whole dwell.
Secure generator and catheter to prevent accidental migration.
documentation: Transvenous pacemaker for unstable bradycardia or conduction disease.
Consent or emergent rationale.
Venous access site and technique, and the reason that site was chosen.
Catheter, generator, and connector cable by name.
Rate, output, threshold, sensitivity, and insertion depth at capture.
Mechanical capture confirmed clinically or hemodynamically.
Securement, imaging, dwell-time plan, and consultation.
seniorPearls: Air in the balloon. Not saline, not contrast.
Write the threshold down.
Keep pads on until the whole setup is stable and secured.
Every movement can lose capture; check after transport.
Spikes without capture at maximum output are a malposition, not a generator problem.

shiftMode: Staff and equip this as an airway procedure.
Adult ED or ICU moderate-to-deep sedation only - not general anesthesia, elective or outpatient sedation, or pediatric sedation.
Patients can go deeper than intended: staff and equip to rescue one level deeper than the target.
A dedicated clinician monitors and does nothing else - the proceduralist can't do it.
Pre-brief airway risk, hemodynamics, meds, dose plan, and rescue plan.
Continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac monitoring, cycled blood pressure, and continuous waveform capnography (required): on supplemental oxygen, saturation lags true oxygenation by minutes.
Suction, BVM, airway adjuncts, and reversal/rescue meds physically in the room.
Dose to patient response.
indications: Painful or anxiety-provoking procedure requiring controlled sedation
Reduction, cardioversion, abscess drainage, chest tube, complex wound care
Facilitation of urgent imaging/procedure when benefits outweigh risk
contraindications: Major cautions: high aspiration risk, difficult airway, severe physiologic instability, inadequate staffing or equipment
Agent-specific contraindications by medication and physiology
Urgent sedation is not delayed for fasting time.

Elective sedation is a different decision. Full-stomach risk, urgent or elective - bowel obstruction, active vomiting, upper GI bleeding, late pregnancy, obtundation, gastroparesis, or a GLP-1 receptor agonist: adjust depth, agent, airway plan, or whether to sedate at all; fasting time alone does not decide it.
Adult scope only. Pediatric sedation - different agents, routes, monitoring intervals, and discharge rules - is not covered.
anatomy: Airway patency, respiratory drive, and hemodynamic reserve.
Know whether the patient will be supine, lateral, or immobilized.
equipment: Cardiac monitor, pulse oximeter, BP cycling
Continuous waveform capnography
Oxygen: nasal cannula/NRB
BVM with mask, PEEP valve if available
Suction connected
Oral/nasal airways
Advanced airway equipment immediately available
Sedative/analgesic medications labeled
Naloxone and flumazenil - doses on the procedural sedation apnea rescue card.
IV access
Procedure equipment ready before sedation
positioning: Position for airway access and the procedure
Preoxygenate when risk is meaningful
Remove loose dentures/foreign bodies if appropriate
steps: Assess indication, comorbidities, allergies, ASA-style risk, and the airway: mouth opening, thyromental distance, neck movement, obesity, beard, obstructive sleep apnea, any previous difficult airway.
Consent and time-out.
Assign sedation monitor and proceduralist roles.
Prepare airway/rescue equipment before medications.
If the procedure includes infiltration or a block, calculate the maximum local anesthetic dose first. Sedation does not change the maximum, and a sedated patient cannot report early toxicity.
Dose incrementally; wait for peak effect before redosing.
Continuously monitor ventilation, oxygenation, perfusion, and procedural conditions.
Treat airway obstruction or apnea immediately.
Observe until back to baseline and discharge/admission criteria are met.
confirmation: Adequate procedural conditions
Ventilation maintained by ETCO2/chest rise
Oxygenation maintained
Hemodynamics acceptable
Baseline mental status and airway function before discharge
troubleshooting: Apnea: stop dosing, jaw thrust, suction, airway adjunct, BVM/PEEP, prepare intubation.

Laryngospasm: stridor, or silent obstruction with paradoxical chest movement. Remove the stimulus; 100% oxygen by tight-fitting mask with jaw thrust and CPAP-level pressure; if it does not break, subparalyzing succinylcholine. Doses on the laryngospasm rescue card.
Vomiting: head down and turned to the side, suction under direct vision, stop the procedure. Do not blindly instrument the airway.
Hypotension: stop sedative, fluids/pressors, reassess bleeding/sepsis/agent effect.
Emergence/agitation: reduce stimulation, protect patient, agent-specific management.
Inadequate sedation: pause, reassess analgesia vs sedation, redose deliberately.
aftercare: Recover in a monitored area with the same monitoring; reassess at defined intervals.
Discharge criteria, all of them: back to baseline mental status, protecting their own airway, vital signs at baseline, pain controlled, and moving at their usual level.
After naloxone or flumazenil, extend the observation period. Both wear off before the drug they reversed - roughly a two-hour window in which resedation can occur.
Outpatient: written discharge precautions and a responsible adult; no driving, machinery, alcohol, or important decisions for 24 hours.
documentation: Procedural sedation for the documented procedure.
Consent; risks/benefits discussed when feasible.
Pre- and post-sedation assessment.
Monitoring: cardiac, pulse oximetry, blood pressure, continuous waveform capnography.
Sedation medications, doses, and times.
Tolerance; complications - airway and hemodynamic events with interventions.
Recovery to baseline before disposition.
seniorPearls: Do not start the procedure before the room is ready.
ETCO2 shows hypoventilation early; pulse oximetry shows it late.
Choose the sedative you know how to rescue from.

medicationDosing.indication: Adult procedural sedation. Doses are targets titrated to effect, not ceilings, and are lower than the induction doses on the intubation card.
medicationDosing.inductionRequirement: Be able to rescue a patient one level deeper than you intend. Propofol and dissociative-dose ketamine can both produce general anesthesia, so the room must be staffed and equipped to manage an apneic, unprotected airway before the first milliliter goes in.

medications.caution: Give over 1-2 minutes; a rapid push causes apnea. Dissociation is all or nothing, so an underdose does not give light sedation - it gives an agitated, undissociated patient. Increases secretions and is the agent most associated with laryngospasm: have suction in hand. No reversal agent exists. Intramuscular 4-5 mg/kg is an option without IV access, with slower onset and longer recovery.

medications.durationNote: lasts 5-10 min; redose 0.25-0.5 mg/kg every 1-3 min
medications.caution: Apnea and hypotension are expected effects at these doses, not complications. No analgesia - pair it with an analgesic for a painful procedure. Dose on lean body weight and reduce it in the elderly or hypovolemic.

This is roughly half the intubation induction dose in this app - check which card you are reading. Myoclonus is common and can be mistaken for a seizure or for inadequate sedation; treating it with more etomidate is the wrong move.
Slow to peak. Wait the full 2-5 minutes before redosing or you will stack doses. Synergistic with opioids for apnea: reduce both when they are combined.
Analgesia, not sedation. Combined with any sedative the risk of apnea is more than additive, so reduce both. Chest wall rigidity is rare but occurs with rapid high-dose administration.

selectionGuidance: Brief and painful, hemodynamics uncertain: ketamine.
Brief and not painful, patient stable: propofol.
Painful, and you want analgesia separate from sedation: an opioid plus a reduced dose of a sedative.
Hemodynamically fragile and sedation is unavoidable: etomidate at the sedation dose above.
Anxiolysis only, with no procedural pain: midazolam alone.
medicationDosing.sourceNote: Conventional adult emergency-department sedation doses, accepted by the clinical owner on 2026-07-30. The ASA and ACEP guidelines in this record's references govern staffing, monitoring, depth, and fasting rather than specific doses; the figures here are widely used starting points for titration in a monitored patient, not a protocol, and are not independently verified against a primary pharmacology source. Paediatric sedation is out of scope for this card.

shiftMode: Suspected bacterial meningitis: antibiotics first. Imaging, positioning, consent, and tubes do not delay the first dose.
Blood cultures before antibiotics; the LP can follow. CSF cell count, glucose, protein, and PCR remain useful after the first dose; culture may not.
Suspected meningitis: check blood glucose immediately before the LP - the CSF:blood glucose ratio needs a paired value.
Positioning decides success: flex well, no rotation.
L3-L4 or L4-L5; not higher.
Atraumatic pencil-point needle is the default; it needs an introducer.
Opening pressure: tubes labeled and manometer assembled before puncture.
Traumatic or no flow: pause and reposition; do not dig.
Document the neurological examination before local anesthetic when feasible.
indications: Suspected meningitis or encephalitis
Subarachnoid hemorrhage after a negative CT outside the window in which CT alone is sufficient
Opening pressure measurement
Diagnostic CSF studies: inflammatory, malignant, infectious
Therapeutic CSF removal where agreed, as in idiopathic intracranial hypertension
contraindications: Image the head first, and treat first, with any of: focal neurological deficit, new-onset seizure, reduced or fluctuating conscious level, papilledema, abnormal pupils, abnormal posturing, or significant immunocompromise (mass lesion or impending herniation likely). Routine CT for everyone is not indicated.
Deferring the LP for imaging never defers the antibiotics.
Shock, respiratory compromise, uncontrolled seizures, or an unstable patient who cannot tolerate positioning: stabilize first, LP later. Positioning alone can be lethal in a marginal patient.

Coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia, or therapeutic anticoagulation: neuraxial procedure, concealed bleed. Follow a named local antithrombotic policy - the hold interval depends on agent, dose, renal function, and urgency. A coagulopathy that defers the LP does not defer antibiotics.
Infection at the puncture site
Adult scope. Pediatric and neonatal LP differ in interspace, needle length, sedation, CSF volume, and opening-pressure interpretation - not covered.
anatomy: The intercristal (Tuffier's) line approximates the L4 spinous process but sits higher than expected in obesity and pregnancy. If the level matters, count up from the sacrum or mark the interspace with ultrasound.
Midline between spinous processes, aimed toward the umbilicus.
Conus usually ends above adult L3; use lower lumbar spaces.
equipment: LP tray
Sterile gloves, surgical mask, prep, drape
Atraumatic pencil-point spinal needle, 22-25 gauge, with its introducer - the default for adults
Cutting (Quincke) needle as fallback when no atraumatic needle is stocked
Longer needle for large body habitus
Manometer and three-way tap for opening pressure
Collection tubes labeled 1-4
1% lidocaine and a small needle
Bandage
Assistant for positioning
positioning: Lateral decubitus for opening pressure; hips and neck flexed, airway comfortable.
Sitting-flexed improves success and midline identification but makes opening pressure uninterpretable.
Shoulders and hips perpendicular to the bed; back plane vertical, not rolled.
Needle in, before measuring: let the legs come down. Flexion falsely raises the opening pressure.
steps: Suspected meningitis: blood cultures, then antibiotics, then everything below.
Review contraindications and imaging criteria; consent; confirm required studies.
Position, identify the interspace, mark it.
Prep and drape.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue.
Introducer first, then the atraumatic needle through it, angled slightly cephalad. Bevel orientation is a cutting-needle instruction and does not apply to a pencil-point needle.
Advance slowly. An atraumatic needle gives a subtle or absent pop - remove the stylet to check for flow every few millimeters.
Measure opening pressure before removing any CSF: lateral, legs and neck relaxed, manometer zeroed at the interspace.
Collect CSF in ordered tubes.
Replace the stylet before withdrawing; dress the site; reassess the neurological examination.
ultrasound: Marks midline and depth in obese or difficult anatomy; most useful before the first attempt.
confirmation: CSF sent for ordered studies
Opening pressure measured before CSF removal; record position, leg position, and zero reference beside the number. Commonly cited adult range about 6-25 cmH2O.
Straining, coughing, Valsalva, hypercapnia, and flexion all raise it; a single high reading in a struggling patient does not establish intracranial hypertension.
Neurologic status reassessed
Tube numbers and appearance documented
troubleshooting: No CSF: recheck position, level, angle, depth; longer needle or ultrasound marking.
Repeated bone: withdraw to subcutaneous tissue and redirect slightly cephalad.
Flow starts then stops: rotate the needle 90 degrees - a nerve root or the arachnoid can occlude the aperture. Rotate, do not advance.
Traumatic tap: minimize needle movement; another level if needed.
Post-LP headache: counsel, fluids/analgesia, blood patch pathway if persistent or severe.
aftercare: Bed rest does not prevent post-dural-puncture headache. Lying flat may ease an established one; do not offer it as prophylaxis.
Send CSF promptly, correctly labeled and ordered.
Reassess neuro status and puncture site.
New or worsening back pain, leg weakness, numbness, or urinary retention after an LP: treat as spinal or epidural hematoma - urgent MRI and neurosurgery.
Hematoma risk is highest if anticoagulated or coagulopathic; decompression preserves function only within hours.
Return precautions: severe headache, fever, weakness, urinary retention, site problems.
documentation: Lumbar puncture indication.
Consent; contraindications and imaging criteria reviewed.
Suspected meningitis: times of blood cultures, first antibiotic dose, and LP.
Position and sterile technique.
Needle type (atraumatic or cutting), gauge, and level.
CSF obtained, or unsuccessful attempts.
Opening pressure with position, leg position, and zero reference, if measured.
CSF appearance, tubes, studies; tolerance and complications.
seniorPearls: Most failed LPs are positioning failures.
Repeated bone: withdraw and reset the angle; do not go deeper.
Label tubes before you are holding CSF.

visualAssets.title: LP interspace landmarks
visualAssets.subtitle: Tuffier's line (a line connecting the iliac crests) crosses at approximately the L4 spinous process. L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspaces are the target, below the conus medullaris.
visualAssets.caption: Left lateral decubitus from behind, head to the right: Tuffier's line joins the iliac crests at about L4; target L3-L4 or L4-L5.

visualAssets.title: Needle trajectory
visualAssets.subtitle: Midline approach: needle angled slightly cephalad, passing through skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, then dura. Pop felt at dura entry.
visualAssets.caption: Midline sagittal section, head to the right: needle angled slightly cephalad through the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum and dura into the CSF.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: If bone is hit, withdraw and redirect — do not force through.

shiftMode: Confirm indication, site preference, and assess collateral flow with ultrasound before committing.
Position wrist in 20-30° extension over a firm roll; tape securely without restricting distal circulation.
Use ultrasound to identify radial artery, confirm pulsatility and depth.
Anesthetize even in awake patients — unanesthetized puncture causes movement and failed placement.
Advance catheter-over-needle bevel-up at 30-45°; on flashback, flatten and advance. Use Seldinger for deep or small vessels.
Arterial waveform on the transducer is definitive confirmation — flat or venous tracing means reposition or replace.
Label, zero at the phlebostatic axis, square-wave test before trusting readings. Re-level after every bed height change.
Titrate to MAP.
indications: Continuous beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring in hemodynamic instability or vasopressor titration
Frequent arterial blood gas sampling (>4-6 ABGs anticipated)
Non-invasive BP unreliable due to arrhythmia, severe hypotension, obesity, or peripheral vascular disease
High-risk procedures, RSI, or sedation requiring real-time hemodynamic monitoring
contraindications: No identifiable arterial signal at planned site.
Relative — Raynaud phenomenon, limb ischemia, or insufficient collateral flow.
Active infection, burn, or wound overlying the insertion site
Suspected arterial disease, thrombosis, or prior catheterization damage at site
Severe coagulopathy
anatomy: Radial artery runs along the lateral volar forearm, superficial to the flexor carpi radialis tendon; typically 2-4 mm diameter at 3-8 mm depth.
Dual radial-ulnar supply provides collateral protection; assess with ultrasound if perfusion uncertain.
Femoral offers larger target but higher infection and noncompressible-bleeding risk.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial are alternatives when upper extremities are inaccessible.
Artery is pulsatile and non-compressible; distinguish clearly from the adjacent cephalic vein.
equipment: Arterial catheter kit (Arrow) or 20-gauge catheter-over-needle with Seldinger wire
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5%
Cap, mask, sterile gloves, and a sterile fenestrated drape; full maximal barriers for femoral or axillary placement
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small-gauge needle
Arm board or rolled towel for wrist positioning
Tape for securement
Arterial pressure transducer and tubing with NS flush bag pressurized to 300 mmHg
Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Clear occlusive dressing
Suture or adhesive securement device per preference
Monitor with arterial waveform capability
positioning: Extend wrist 20-30° over a firm roll (rolled towel or IV bag) with the volar surface facing up.
Tape hand and forearm securely to arm board; prevent movement without restricting distal perfusion.
Abduct arm and position ultrasound screen in direct line of sight before prep.
steps: Confirm indication, check for contraindications, and obtain consent if non-emergent.
Set up pressure transducer and tubing; connect to monitor and zero at the phlebostatic axis.
Position wrist over roll in 20-30° extension; secure with tape.
With ultrasound, identify artery, confirm pulsatility, estimate depth, and plan entry point.
Prep skin widely with chlorhexidine; apply sterile drape.
Infiltrate skin and subcutaneous tissue with local anesthetic along the planned tract.
With ultrasound guidance, advance needle at 30-45° bevel-up; watch for pulsatile flash.

On flash: for catheter-over-needle (Arrow kit) — flatten slightly, advance catheter off needle, remove needle. for Seldinger — flatten, pass wire without force, remove needle, thread catheter over wire, remove wire.
Connect arterial tubing; confirm arterial waveform on monitor.
Secure catheter, apply clear dressing, and label with site and date.

Perform a square-wave (fast-flush) test before treating any displayed number: one to two oscillations back to baseline is adequate; more than two with sharp overshoot is underdamped and reads systolic too high; a slurred return with no oscillation is overdamped and reads systolic too low.
Until the trace passes that test, titrate vasoactives to MAP rather than systolic and correlate against a cuff.
ultrasound: Short-axis approach: confirm artery is pulsatile and non-compressible; distinguish from adjacent vein.
Long-axis approach: useful for visualizing needle trajectory and catheter advancement.
Confirm wire position in vessel lumen before advancing catheter with Seldinger technique.
Post-placement: assess distal perfusion if any concern about thrombosis or vasospasm.
confirmation: Pulsatile arterial waveform visible on bedside monitor
Bright red flash at time of needle entry
Catheter flushes smoothly with no resistance
Catheter secured and labeled; transducer zeroed
Square-wave test performed and the trace judged adequately damped
Flush system continuously pressurized at ~300 mmHg
troubleshooting: Flash without waveform: check transducer connections, tubing, and zero; re-advance catheter slightly or retry Seldinger.
Catheter will not advance over needle: do not force; switch to Seldinger technique or resite.

Overdamped (slurred square-wave return, systolic reads low): hunt air bubbles in the tubing and transducer first, then tip clot, kink, loose connection, flush bag below 300 mmHg, or over-long compliant tubing.

Underdamped or resonant (more than two oscillations, systolic reads high by 20-30 mmHg): shorten the circuit, remove unnecessary stopcocks, consider a damping device. Expect it in tachycardic, hyperdynamic patients.
Displayed pressure does not fit the patient: re-level at the phlebostatic axis, repeat the square-wave test, and compare with a cuff. A transducer 10 cm off is about 7.5 mmHg of error.
Loss of signal with movement: improve limb securement and confirm catheter is not kinked.
Hematoma: remove catheter, hold firm pressure ≥5 min, and check distal perfusion.
complications: Thrombosis with distal ischemia — remove catheter immediately if suspected
Infection - risk rises with femoral site, longer dwell, and emergent insertion, not with a fixed number of hours
aftercare: Remove catheter as soon as hemodynamic monitoring is no longer required.
Hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes after removal.
Assess distal perfusion and capillary refill after removal.
documentation: Arterial line site [radial/femoral/dorsalis pedis] and indication.
Consent, or emergent need if not possible.
Ultrasound guidance; artery confirmed by pulsatility and non-compressibility.
Technique [catheter-over-needle / Seldinger].
Arterial waveform confirmed on monitor; transducer zeroed.
Catheter secured with clear dressing, labeled with date and site.
Distal perfusion intact after placement.
seniorPearls: A firm, secure 20-30 degree wrist extension improves first-pass success.
Seldinger technique outperforms catheter-over-needle in patients with deep, small, or difficult vessels.
Fix or replace a persistently damped line rather than accept inaccurate readings. Underdamping is the more dangerous direction - it hides hypotension behind a falsely reassuring systolic.
references: CDC. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections: arterial catheters and pressure-monitoring systems. 2011 guideline, page updated 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html - prompt removal when monitoring is no longer needed is the only measure that reliably lowers infection.

shiftMode: Confirm indication and laterality; verify on ultrasound that the effusion is free-flowing, not loculated.
Mark the site with the patient in the procedure position.
Puncture over the superior margin of the lower rib.
Anesthetize down to the pleural surface.
For therapeutic drainage: connect the collection system before advancing the catheter, to keep air out.
Drain to until symptoms improve. Then stop and clamp.

Stop if the patient begins to repetitively cough, have chest tightness, or worsening dyspnea - preceding re-expansion pulmonary edema.

General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.

Once finished, check lung sliding on ultrasound.

Only check CXR if — symptomatic, air was aspirated, sliding is absent/uncertain, or the patient is ventilated or can't report symptoms.
indications: Evaluation of a new, undiagnosed pleural effusion
Therapeutic relief of respiratory compromise from a large pleural effusion
Evaluation of parapneumonic effusion for empyema, complicated effusion, or effusion requiring drainage
contraindications: Patient unable to remain still during procedure (relative; consider procedural sedation)
Uncorrected coagulopathy with significant bleeding risk
Effusion too small or clearly loculated with no safe accessible pocket
Pneumothorax with effusion, or hydropneumothorax (requires chest tube)
Known lung adherence to chest wall at the planned site
anatomy: Pleural space lies between parietal and visceral pleura.
Intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove of each rib in the order vein, artery, nerve (VAN) from superior to inferior. Puncture over the superior margin of the lower rib.
Diaphragm rises during expiration and varies with body habitus.
Right-sided approach: liver is at risk below the 9th rib posteriorly.
Left-sided approach: spleen is at risk.
equipment: Thoracentesis kit (needle, catheter, three-way stopcock, 60 mL syringe)
Ultrasound machine
Chlorhexidine prep
Sterile drape, sterile gloves, mask
Local anesthetic (1% lidocaine), syringe, and 22-25 gauge anesthesia needle
Drainage tubing with a three-way stopcock for manual syringe aspiration, or a gravity bag hung below the patient. Vacuum bottles and wall suction are not used for therapeutic aspiration.
Plain specimen containers (LDH, protein, glucose, cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and cytology)
Blood culture bottles inoculated at the bedside in addition to plain containers (if pleural infection is suspected)
Heparinized blood-gas syringe for pleural pH, analyzed immediately on a gas analyser
Occlusive dressing
Drainage measurement container
positioning:
Seated and leaning forward over a padded bedside table with arms resting on a pillow — 

drops the scapula and opens interspaces for posterior access.

Supine with ipsilateral arm raised overhead —

acceptable for ventilated or unable-to-sit patients.
steps: Confirm the effusion side, size, and indication.
Obtain consent when feasible.
Perform ultrasound with patient in procedure position; identify the optimal fluid pocket and mark the entry site.
Prep and drape the posterior-lateral chest at the marked site.
Anesthetize skin, subcutaneous tissue, rib periosteum, and pleural surface. Aspirate as you advance.
Insert the procedure needle along the superior margin of the lower rib with continuous aspiration.
On pleural fluid return, lock needle position. If collecting for diagnostic aspiration, collect 30-60 mL.
For therapeutic aspiration: advance catheter over needle or via Seldinger technique, then connect drainage tubing to prevent air entry.
Drain by manual syringe aspiration through the stopcock, or by gravity to a bag below the patient. Monitor symptoms continuously.
Drain to symptoms. Stop and clamp for repetitive cough, chest tightness, or worsening dyspnea.
Withdraw catheter/needle at end of expiration or with patient performing Valsalva; apply occlusive dressing immediately.
Check lung sliding on ultrasound immediately.
ultrasound: Low-frequency curvilinear or phased-array probe in the posterior-lateral chest to identify the effusion.
Confirm fluid is anechoic/hypoechoic and free-flowing with respiration. Loculations = hyperechoic strands.
Measure the largest pocket depth and distance from skin to fluid.
confirmation: Pleural fluid aspirated freely and consistent with expected character
No sudden air return
Respiratory symptoms improved
Lung sliding present on immediate post-procedure ultrasound
Specimens labeled and sent promptly
troubleshooting: No fluid on aspiration: Pocket may have shifted, use ultrasound.
Air return: withdraw immediately, needle may be in lung parenchyma, assess for pneumothorax.
Bloody return: Hemorrhagic effusion vs. hemothorax vs. vessel injury — non-clotting blood suggests pleural; rapidly clotting blood suggests vascular.
Repetitive cough, chest tightness, or worsening dyspnea during drainage: stop and clamp. General ceiling is 1.5 L in one session.
Loculated pocket: scan multiple windows, consult interventional radiology or thoracics if no pocket.
aftercare: Monitor O2 saturation, respiratory rate, and breath sounds for ≥1 hour after procedure.
Immediate lung ultrasound for sliding in everyone.

Pleural pH goes in a heparinized blood-gas syringe and is analyzed immediately: lidocaine contamination and excess heparin both falsely lower it. 

Do not send pH on frank pus.
Record total volume drained and fluid character.
documentation: Thoracentesis at [right/left], [interspace], for [indication].
Consent, or emergent need.
Ultrasound for site selection and real-time guidance.
[Volume] mL of [serous/serosanguineous/purulent] fluid drained; no air return.
Specimens sent for [LDH, protein, cell count, culture, cytology as ordered].
Post-procedure imaging: [result, e.g., no pneumothorax, residual small effusion].
Procedure tolerated without oxygen desaturation, respiratory distress, or significant bleeding.
seniorPearls: Mark the site with the patient in the procedure position.
Most missed pneumothoraces are in ventilated or obtunded patients who cannot report symptoms.
Stop before 1.5 L unless you have a compelling reason and are monitoring closely for re-expansion pulmonary edema

Take the lower figure - this is a wide infiltration of skin, periosteum and pleura in a patient who may already be hypoxic.

Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.

shiftMode: Confirm indication (diagnostic vs therapeutic) and accessible ascites on ultrasound.
Ultrasound-mark the largest, safest LLQ pocket, clear of bowel, bladder, and inferior epigastric vessels.
Over 5 L: albumin 6-8 g per liter removed, to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction.
Under 5 L: albumin is not routine; consider it for acute-on-chronic liver failure or high AKI risk. Clinical judgement, no fixed volume threshold.
Every hospitalized cirrhotic with ascites who decompensates needs a diagnostic tap.
Inoculate blood culture bottles at the bedside from the first 10-20 mL drawn - highest yield for SBP.
Do not delay or cancel the tap to correct clotting numbers.
indications: New-onset ascites
Suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in any hospitalized patient with cirrhosis and ascites
Therapeutic large-volume paracentesis for tense or symptomatic ascites causing respiratory compromise or discomfort
Ascites in acute decompensated liver disease, malignancy, or unknown etiology
contraindications: Disseminated intravascular coagulation or clinically active bleeding
Surgical abdomen with possible bowel perforation at all accessible sites
Infection, wound, or burn over all potential insertion sites
Adhesions or bowel loops adherent to the anterior abdominal wall at the planned site

No INR or platelet threshold applies. Guidance recommends against routine coagulation testing and prophylactic plasma or platelets before paracentesis; the INR does not describe bleeding risk in cirrhosis. Assess bleeding risk clinically; follow local procedural policy.
anatomy: Standard entry: LLQ, more than two-thirds of the way from the midline to the ASIS - lateral to the rectus sheath.
RLQ if LLQ is unsafe (prior surgery, ostomy, other anatomy).
Avoid the midline: diastasis, recanalized umbilical vein, thin soft tissue.
Inferior epigastric vessels run cephalocaudally about 40% of the way from the midline to the ASIS - an entry midway between umbilicus and ASIS can land on them. Confirm with Doppler.
Ultrasound-guided entry is standard of care.
equipment: Paracentesis kit or 18-gauge needle/catheter, three-way stopcock, 60 mL syringe (diagnostic)
Long catheter or pigtail drain for therapeutic drainage >1 L
Ultrasound
Chlorhexidine prep
Sterile drape and gloves
1% lidocaine, syringe, small-gauge needle
Large-bore drainage tubing and collection containers (therapeutic)
Specimen tubes: cell count with differential, ascitic albumin, protein, LDH, glucose, culture
Paired serum albumin drawn at the same time - the serum-ascites albumin gradient needs both values in any new or undifferentiated ascites
Blood culture bottles for bedside inoculation
Occlusive dressing or small bandage
positioning: Supine, slight left lateral decubitus (left side down) to pool ascites in the LLQ.
Head of bed 30° if the patient cannot lie flat.
Empty the bladder first - Foley or void.
steps: Confirm indication and approach; verify ascites on ultrasound.
Empty bladder; slight left lateral decubitus.
Consent when feasible; document emergent need when not.
Real-time ultrasound: choose the pocket in the LLQ or RLQ; mark the entry site.
Prep and drape.
Anesthetize skin, subcutaneous tissue, and peritoneum, aspirating as you advance.
Z-track: displace skin 1-2 cm laterally, insert perpendicular with continuous aspiration, release after entering the peritoneum.
On fluid return, lock the needle or advance the catheter; note fluid character.
Diagnostic: collect 30-60 mL, inoculate blood culture bottles at the bedside, send labelled specimens with a paired serum albumin.
Therapeutic: connect drainage tubing; gravity or low-pressure drainage.
Over 5 L: albumin 6-8 g per liter removed, during or immediately after drainage. Under 5 L: give it for acute-on-chronic liver failure or high acute kidney injury risk; record the reason either way.
Withdraw; brief firm pressure; occlusive dressing.
Monitor BP, HR, and symptoms for 30-60 minutes.
ultrasound: Curvilinear or low-frequency probe: largest free-flowing pocket in the LLQ.
Confirm skin-to-fluid depth and no bowel in the path.
Color Doppler at the planned site for the inferior epigastric vessels.
Scan and mark in the procedure position - fluid redistributes when position changes.
Post-procedure: brief scan for residual ascites and entry-site hematoma.
confirmation: Fluid returns freely on aspiration and during drainage - straw-colored, turbid, milky, or bloody
No bowel contents (feculent material, food particles)
Distension and discomfort reduce during therapeutic drainage
Albumin decision recorded - volume and dose given, or reason withheld
troubleshooting: No fluid: recheck with ultrasound; the needle may have bypassed the pocket - withdraw and reassess live.
Bowel contents: withdraw immediately; watch for peritonitis; most isolated needle punctures of bowel are self-limiting.
Catheter clogs: reposition the patient slightly, flush, replace if blocked.
Persistent site leak: hold pressure; purse-string suture rarely required.
Neutrophils >250/mm³ with suspected SBP: treat empirically pending culture.
complications: Paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (large volume without albumin)
aftercare: Albumin: confirm it was given above 5 L and that the below-5-L decision was recorded. Reassess BP and HR at 1 hour.
After a large-volume tap, check renal function and electrolytes in acute-on-chronic liver failure, baseline renal impairment, or hypotension during drainage.
Send specimens promptly.
Watch for abdominal pain, fever, or hematoma for 4-6 hours.
Return precautions: worsening pain, fever, spreading redness, site leak.
documentation: Paracentesis at [LLQ/RLQ] for [indication].
Consent obtained / emergent need documented.
Ultrasound-guided; pocket at [site].
[Volume] mL of [character] peritoneal fluid removed; total volume and character recorded.
Specimens: [cell count, albumin, protein, LDH, culture, cytology as ordered]; blood culture bottles inoculated at bedside.
Albumin [X g per liter / not indicated - volume <5 L].
Hemodynamically stable post-procedure; no abdominal rigidity or signs of peritonitis.
seniorPearls: SBP cannot be ruled out on examination.
Z-track offsets the skin and peritoneal punctures so the tract closes on itself; this prevents post-tap leak.
references: European Association for the Study of the Liver. EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines for the management of patients with decompensated cirrhosis. J Hepatol. 2018;69(2):406-460. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhep.2018.03.024

American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases. Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Management of Ascites, Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis and Hepatorenal Syndrome. https://www.aasld.org/practice-guidelines/diagnosis-evaluation-and-management-ascites-spontaneous-bacterial-peritonitis

Aithal GP, et al. Guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis. British Society of Gastroenterology and British Association for the Study of the Liver. Gut. 2021;70(1):9-29. https://doi.org/10.1136/gutjnl-2020-321790
Epstein J, Arora A, Ellis H. Surface anatomy of the inferior epigastric artery in relation to laparoscopic injury. Clin Anat. 2004;17(5):400-408. https://doi.org/10.1002/ca.10192
Verify local procedural policy on periprocedural coagulation assessment and the albumin preparation stocked.
