shiftMode: Confirm this is a fluctuant abscess, not cellulitis, a lipoma, or a lymph node.
Anesthetize generously before incising - acidic pus inactivates local anesthetic near the core; infiltrate widely around the margin and wait.
Be sure to have the incision span the entire fluctuant cavity and allow complete drainage and loculation breakdown.
Break down all loculations and irrigate.
For a simple abscess < 5cm, packing not advised. Leave it open, or use a loop drain where the cavity or the site makes premature closure likely.
Primary closure is contraindicated - leave it open.
Antibiotics are a shared decision rather than a reflex in either direction.
indications: Fluctuant, loculated skin or soft tissue abscess confirmed clinically or by ultrasound
Infected sebaceous cyst, pilonidal abscess, or other skin abscess requiring drainage
Paronychia with subungual extension unresponsive to soaking
contraindications: Tissue not clearly fluctuant and abscess not confirmed — do not incise cellulitis blindly
Hand deep-space infection (flexor tenosynovitis risk) — surgical consultation required
Facial abscess near the dangerous triangle or other high-risk vascular territory — surgical consultation preferred
Pain out of proportion, crepitus, skin necrosis, rapid spread (signs of NSTI) — this is a surgical emergency, not a bedside I&D
Abscess adjacent to neurovascular structures or deep fascia without adequate training and imaging
anatomy: Identify abscess boundaries by palpation and ultrasound; plan incision at point of maximal fluctuance.
Avoid crossing joint lines, tendon sheaths, or neurovascular structures with the incision when possible.
Satellite collections are common — explore and break down connecting loculations with blunt dissection.
Perirectal and ischiorectal abscesses require colorectal or surgical expertise; do not attempt without proper training.
Avoid end-arterial zones (fingertip, toe, pinna, nasal tip, penis) with epinephrine-containing anesthetic.
equipment: Scalpel with #11 or #15 blade
Iris scissors and curved hemostat for blunt dissection
Irrigation syringe and normal saline, if irrigating
Splash guard or angiocatheter tip for directed irrigation
Loop drain (Penrose or vessel loop) or plain strip gauze packing, where indicated
Sterile gloves and sterile drape
Chlorhexidine or betadine prep
Local anesthetic: 1% lidocaine with or without epinephrine or regional block
Non-adherent wound dressing and tape
Wound cultures if immunocompromise, recurrence, or systemic infection suspected
positioning: Position the abscess for optimal visualization — often lateral decubitus for buttock or perianal.
Use a headlamp or task light so the depth of the cavity is visible.
Pediatric patients may require restraint assistance or procedural sedation for larger abscesses.
steps: Confirm diagnosis with exam and ultrasound; identify all pockets, satellite collections, and the point of maximal fluctuance.
Infiltrate local anesthetic widely around and beneath the abscess margin - not into the cavity. Allow adequate time for onset (2-3 minutes minimum).
Optionally consider regional nerve block for large or anatomically favorable abscesses.
Prep the area; apply sterile drape.
Make a single, adequate linear incision through the abscess dome at maximal fluctuance - it must be long enough to allow complete drainage and instrument access.
Gently express contents; do not squeeze forcefully.
Insert closed hemostat, open along cavity axis, and sweep to break down all loculations - confirm cavity extent.
Irrigate if the cavity is grossly contaminated or full of debris. No fixed volume, and no need to irrigate until the return runs clear.
Decide on a drain. Use a loop drain for larger or deeper cavities, or where the skin will close over the space before it fills in. If you pack, pack loosely.
Apply non-adherent dressing.
Plan follow-up at 48-72 hours for drain assessment or wound check.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe (10+ MHz) for soft tissue abscess identification.
Confirms hypoechoic or anechoic fluid cavity with posterior acoustic enhancement and internal debris.
Color Doppler identifies adjacent vessels before incision.
Reveals hidden loculations and satellite pockets that palpation alone misses.
Use ultrasound to guide needle aspiration for depth confirmation before incision in deep or uncertain abscesses.
confirmation: Frank pus drains freely on incision
All loculations broken down and cavity fully explored with instrument
Cavity left open, or a loop drain or loose packing placed where indicated - not tight, not obliterating the cavity
No evidence of deeper structure involvement (tendon, joint, fascia)
troubleshooting: No pus on incision: reassess with ultrasound — may have incised into cellulitis or missed the pocket; do not extend blindly.
Bleeding during incision: direct pressure; abscess-bed bleeding is usually minor and self-limited.
Inadequate anesthesia despite infiltration: add more anesthetic outside the margin, wait longer; acidic purulent environment inactivates local anesthetic near the core.
Deep pocket inaccessible: ultrasound-guided aspiration to confirm location; surgical consultation if complex anatomy or uncertain.
Recurrence at same site: consider incomplete drainage, retained foreign body, hidradenitis suppurativa, Crohn's disease, or resistant organism.
complications: Abscess recurrence from inadequate drainage or premature closure
Bacteremia (rare with simple abscess; consider antibiotics if systemic signs develop)
Injury to adjacent neurovascular structures if anatomy is not respected
aftercare: Instruct patient on wound care: warm soaks or showering; keep the site clean and moist.
Return visit in 48-72 hours for drain assessment and wound inspection.

Antibiotics are not a default. Drainage alone cures most simple abscesses. Antibiotics are clearly indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunocompromise, a facial or hand location, or a prosthesis nearby.
Where antibiotics are given, choose against local resistance patterns and cover MRSA where prevalence warrants it.
Return precautions: worsening pain, fever, spreading redness, or red streaking.
documentation: Abscess incision and drainage performed at [site and description] for [indication].
Ultrasound performed: [confirmed abscess / depth / satellite collections noted].
Local anesthetic with [agent/concentration] administered; patient reported adequate analgesia.
[Character and estimated volume of pus] evacuated; cavity irrigated with normal saline until clear.
Loculations broken down; [loop drain / loose packing] placed.
Cultures [sent / not sent]; antibiotics [prescribed / not prescribed] with rationale documented.
Patient discharged with wound care instructions and 48-72 hour follow-up arranged.
seniorPearls: If you cannot freely break down all loculations, the incision is not long enough.
Irrigation and packing are optional. Breaking down loculations is not.
Packing a small simple abscess is painful and does not improve the outcome.
Acidic pus inactivates local anesthetic near the core, so anesthetic placed into the cavity does nothing.

Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Confirm you need large-bore central access: massive transfusion, rapid volume, or a conduit for a transvenous pacer/PA catheter. A triple lumen isn't interchangeable with an introducer.
Full sterile barrier and ultrasound.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating — arterial dilation with an 8.5 Fr sheath is a surgical emergency.
Dilator and sheath advance as a unit over a free-moving wire; never lose the back end.
Gentle rotation, not force — an inadequate skin nick lets the sheath tip peel back.
Remove dilator and wire together; immediately cap or connect the side port and aspirate/flush.
Confirm position and screen for pneumothorax/arterial placement per site and local policy.
indications: Anticipated massive transfusion or rapid large-volume resuscitation
Conduit for a transvenous pacemaker or pulmonary artery catheter
High-flow access when peripheral large-bore IVs are inadequate or impossible
Hemodynamic instability requiring reliable, high-flow central access
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection, burn, or significant injury overlying the intended site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at the intended vein
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy: relative; weigh against urgency, choose a compressible site
A large introducer where a smaller multi-lumen catheter meets the need
anatomy: IJ and femoral are the usual sites; subclavian/axillary carry higher pneumothorax and noncompressible-bleeding risk with a large sheath.
The vein must comfortably accommodate an 8.5 Fr (or larger) sheath.
IJ: carotid and pleural dome close by at the base of the neck.
equipment: Introducer/Cordis kit: sheath, integrated dilator, guidewire, needle, scalpel. Card matches 8.5-9 Fr, 10 cm percutaneous sheath introducers with hemostasis valve and side arm; for other designs read the insert - assembly and removal sequences vary.
Sterile pressure tubing or manometry to confirm venous placement before dilation
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5%
Ultrasound, sterile probe cover and gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Saline flush for the side port
Suture or securement device and sterile dressing
Sharps container and sterile towels
Chest x-ray for IJ/subclavian/axillary placement
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, neck not over-rotated.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Ultrasound screen in direct line of sight before prep.
steps: Confirm indication; select site by urgency, anatomy, and bleeding risk.
Ultrasound survey before opening the kit: vein caliber, compressibility, patency, trajectory - compressible vein vs pulsatile, noncompressible artery before puncture.
Full sterile barrier prep and drape.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along the tract.
Cannulate under ultrasound, tracking the needle tip.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating: inside the vein, not the artery, on short axis; tracking centrally on long axis. Wire not clearly seen: transduce or use a manometer before dilating.
Blood color and non-pulsatile flow do not confirm venous placement.
Any doubt remaining: pass a small dilator or 18 G catheter over the wire and transduce that before committing the 8.5 Fr dilator. Peri-arrest there is no waveform - use ultrasound.
Nick through the dermis into subcutaneous tissue, blade flat against the wire, cutting away from it. An 8.5 Fr sheath needs a real nick.
Advance dilator and sheath over the wire as a unit, with gentle rotation; do not force.
Remove dilator and wire together, holding the sheath; confirm the wire is out intact.
Aspirate and flush the side port; cap or connect it immediately - never leave the hub open to air.
Secure and apply a sterile dressing.
Confirm position and assess for complications per site and local policy.
ultrasound: Confirm the vein is large enough for the sheath and compresses fully before puncture.
Short axis for vessel ID; long axis to track needle and wire if skilled.
Wire in the vein in two planes before dilating; if not clearly seen, transduce.
IJ: check lung sliding afterward as a quick pneumothorax screen; local confirmation standards still apply.
confirmation: Side port aspirates and flushes easily
Guidewire and dilator removed intact
Sheath secured with sterile dressing
Appropriate imaging/confirmation obtained for the site
No evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; recheck needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Sheath tip peels back or kinks: nick too small - withdraw, enlarge the nick, re-advance over a controlled wire.

Arterial puncture, needle only (18 G or smaller, not dilated): withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. Neck puncture: watch the airway for several hours - a carotid hematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it; do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and call vascular surgery and interventional radiology now. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, hemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Color, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not answer it.
Brisk bleeding around the sheath: pressure, assess coagulopathy, confirm intraluminal placement.

Sudden hypoxia, hypotension, or cardiovascular collapse around an open hub: suspect air embolism - occlude the hub, left lateral decubitus head-down, 100% oxygen, and aspirate from a central lumen if one is in place.
Unstable after placement: pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or progressing shock.
complications: Arterial cannulation with a large-bore sheath (surgical emergency)
Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian/axillary approaches
Hematoma or significant bleeding given the large tract
Air embolism through an uncapped large-bore sheath
Arrhythmia from wire or catheter irritation
aftercare: Side port capped or connected at all times.
Label the sheath and date the dressing per local policy.
Review confirmation imaging before high-risk use where site/policy requires.
Removal: supine or head-down, Valsalva or expiratory hold as the sheath comes out, immediate occlusive dressing, patient flat afterwards.
Most large-bore air embolism happens at removal rather than insertion.
Remove the introducer as soon as large-bore access is no longer required.
Reassess the site for bleeding or hematoma.
documentation: Indication for large-bore access.
Consent, or emergent need if not possible.
Site and side; full sterile barrier precautions.
Ultrasound guidance for vein identification and cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance, removed intact with the dilator.
Side port aspirated and flushed; sheath secured with sterile dressing.
Placement confirmation and immediate complication assessment.
seniorPearls: Dilation is irreversible. Do not dilate unless certain the wire is venous.
An uncapped large-bore sheath is an open conduit for air.
references: American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Central Venous Access 2020. Anesthesiology. 2020;132(1):8-43. https://journals.lww.com/anesthesiology/fulltext/2020/01000/practice_guidelines_for_central_venous_access.9.aspx
Association of Anaesthetists. Safe Vascular Access 2025. Anaesthesia. 2025. https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/anae.16727

Teleflex. Arrow percutaneous sheath introducer product and instructions-for-use reference. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/product-areas/vascular-access/central-access/percutaneous-sheath-introducer/index.html

CDC. Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections: summary of recommendations. 2011 guideline, page updated 2024. https://www.cdc.gov/infection-control/hcp/intravascular-catheter-related-infections/summary-recommendations.html

visualAssets.title: Dilator-sheath assembly
visualAssets.subtitle: The assembled dilator and sheath advance together over a controlled wire, through an adequate skin nick.
visualAssets.caption: Side-on cut-away, any site: dilator tip in the vein, sheath riding behind it through a nick wider than the sheath, wire tail held out of the back of the hub (inset).
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Control the wire at all times; an 8.5 Fr sheath needs a real skin nick.

shiftMode: Confirm the need is dialysis-level flow (urgent HD, CRRT, or plasmapheresis)
Site choice matters: right IJ preferred for function and lower complication; avoid subclavian to preserve future fistula options.
Full sterile barrier and ultrasound.
Pick the length before opening the kit: right IJ 12-15 cm, left IJ 15-20 cm, femoral 19-24 cm.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating.
Dilate sequentially without force — enough to pass the catheter, not over-dilated.
Both lumens must aspirate and flush; lock each to its printed priming volume, and aspirate that lock before next use.
Confirm tip position and screen for complications before the line is used for dialysis.
indications: Urgent or emergent hemodialysis (hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, fluid overload, uremia, certain toxic ingestions)
Continuous renal replacement therapy in the critically ill
Plasmapheresis or therapeutic apheresis requiring high blood flow
Bridge access while definitive dialysis access is established
contraindications: Patient refusal when non-emergent
Infection or burn over the intended site
Thrombosis or distorted anatomy at the intended vein
Subclavian approach is relatively contraindicated in candidates for future AV fistula (stenosis risk)
Uncorrected severe coagulopathy (relative)
anatomy: Right IJ offers the straightest path to the SVC/RA junction and is the preferred site for catheter function.
Femoral is acceptable for short-term or emergent access, with higher infection risk and flow limitations.
Avoid subclavian when possible to preserve the vasculature for future arteriovenous access.
Length by site: right IJ 12-15 cm, left IJ 15-20 cm, femoral 19-24 cm.
equipment: Dialysis catheter kit. Adult catheters are typically 12-14 Fr. pick the length by site before opening the kit.
Sterile pressure tubing or manometry setup to confirm venous placement before dilation
Sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and large sterile drape
Alcoholic chlorhexidine over 0.5%
Ultrasound machine with sterile probe cover and sterile gel
Local anesthetic, syringe, and small needle
Heparin or citrate catheter lock solution.
Sterile saline flushes for both lumens
Suture/securement device and sterile dressing
Confirmation workflow (chest x-ray) for IJ/subclavian placement
positioning: IJ: Trendelenburg if tolerated, head slightly turned away, neck not over-rotated.
Femoral: supine, leg slightly abducted and externally rotated if tolerated.
Place the ultrasound screen in your line of sight before sterile prep.
Optimize lighting and table height before opening the kit.
steps: Confirm dialysis-level indication and select the site, preferring right IJ when feasible.
Ultrasound survey before opening the kit: confirm vein caliber, patency, and trajectory.
Prep and drape with full sterile barrier technique.
Anesthetize skin and deeper tissue along the planned tract.
Cannulate the vein under ultrasound guidance with needle-tip awareness.
Confirm the wire is venous before dilating. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce or manometer before dilating. Blood color and non-pulsatile flow do not confirm venous placement.
Make an adequate skin nick at the wire, controlling the wire at all times.
Pass serial dilators over the wire to develop the tract; advance gently with rotation, never forcing.

Advance the dual-lumen catheter over the wire to the depth planned for that site and catheter length: 
- Right IJ = 12-15 cm
- Left IJ 15-20 cm
- Femoral 19-24 cm
Remove the wire while holding the catheter; confirm the wire is out intact.

Aspirate and flush both lumens, then lock each with the prescribed solution to the priming volume printed on that lumen. Overfilling pushes lock into the patient; underfilling lets blood in and it clots.
Label both lumens as locked so nobody flushes them.
Secure the catheter, apply a sterile dressing, and confirm tip position before dialysis use.
ultrasound: Confirm the vein is large enough and compresses fully before puncture.
Use short-axis for vessel ID; long-axis to track the needle and wire if skilled.
Confirm the guidewire in the vein in two planes before serial dilation. If the wire is not clearly seen, transduce first.
For IJ, check lung sliding afterward as a rapid pneumothorax screen, but follow local confirmation standards.
confirmation: Both arterial and venous lumens aspirate and flush easily
Guidewire and dilators removed intact
Catheter locked with the prescribed solution and volume
Tip position confirmed by imaging before dialysis use (IJ/subclavian)
No evidence of arterial placement, pneumothorax, hematoma, or malposition
troubleshooting: Wire will not pass: stop, do not force; recheck needle position and angle, aspirate, use ultrasound, or repuncture.
Catheter will not advance despite dilation: the tract is under-developed or the wire has kinked; re-dilate over a controlled wire and recheck.

Arterial puncture with the needle only: withdraw and hold firm pressure 5-10 minutes, longer if anticoagulated. After a neck puncture watch the airway for several hours - a carotid hematoma can obstruct late.

Dilator or catheter in an artery, or any device in the subclavian or axillary: leave it in place. Do not remove it and do not compress. Cap or transduce it so it neither bleeds nor entrains air, secure it against dislodgement, and immediately call vascular surgery and interventional radiology. Keep the patient flat and still. Removal with external pressure at a non-compressible site risks stroke, hemothorax, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Unsure whether you are in the artery or the vein: transduce it. Color, non-pulsatile flow, and a blood gas do not answer it.
Poor flow from one lumen after placement: reposition the patient, confirm depth and tip position, and avoid forcing against resistance.
Unstable after placement: consider pneumothorax, bleeding, arrhythmia, air embolism, or progression of underlying illness.
complications: Arterial cannulation with a large-bore catheter
Pneumothorax or hemothorax, especially with IJ/subclavian approaches
Hematoma or significant bleeding from the large tract
Catheter dysfunction or inadequate dialysis flow
Central vein stenosis (notably with subclavian placement)
Air embolism, guidewire loss, arrhythmia, infection, or thrombosis
aftercare: Lock both lumens with the prescribed solution to the printed priming volume, and label them. The lock is aspirated and discarded before every use - never flushed into the patient.
Reserve the catheter for dialysis.
Confirm tip position on imaging before first dialysis run for IJ/subclavian lines.
Remove the catheter as soon as dialysis access is no longer required.
Reassess the site for bleeding, hematoma, or signs of infection.
documentation: Indication for dual-lumen dialysis catheter.
Consent, or emergent need if not possible.
Site and side; full sterile barrier precautions.
Ultrasound guidance for vein identification and cannulation.
Guidewire passed without resistance; serial dilation; wire removed intact.
Both lumens aspirated, flushed, and locked with the prescribed solution and volume.
Tip position confirmation and immediate complication assessment.
seniorPearls: Right IJ to the cavoatrial junction gives the best function; femoral works but flows and infection rates are worse.
Avoid the subclavian in anyone who may ever need a fistula - central stenosis can cost them future access.
If a lumen will not aspirate, do not flush it under pressure; reposition and reconfirm tip position first.
A non-tunnelled IJ catheter is stiff. The tip belongs at the superior vena cava/right atrial junction, not in the atrium, where a stiff tip can perforate.

A femoral catheter that is too short leaves the tip in the iliac vein - poor flows and 
high recirculation.
references: KDIGO. Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury, section 5.4: vascular access for renal replacement therapy. Kidney Int Suppl. 2012;2(1). https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/KDIGO-2012-AKI-Guideline-English.pdf
National Kidney Foundation. KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access: 2019 update. https://www.kidney.org/professionals/kdoqi/guidelines-and-commentaries/vascular-access

American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Central Venous Access 2020. Anesthesiology. 2020;132(1):8-43. https://journals.lww.com/anesthesiology/fulltext/2020/01000/practice_guidelines_for_central_venous_access.9.aspx

Teleflex. Arrow acute hemodialysis catheter specifications and instructions-for-use reference. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/product-areas/vascular-access/central-access/acute-hemodialysis-catheters/
FDA. DefenCath (taurolidine and heparin) prescribing information, illustrating lock-volume and aspiration requirements. 2023. https://www.fda.gov/media/179230/download

visualAssets.title: Catheter tip position
visualAssets.subtitle: Right IJ trajectory to the cavoatrial junction and dual-lumen orientation.
visualAssets.caption: Front view in chest X-ray orientation: the patient's right is on the image left.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: The tip belongs at the superior vena cava/right atrial junction, not in the atrium.

shiftMode: Measure depth before picking the catheter — too deep and it won't seat.
Avoid the brachial artery and median nerve in the medial upper arm; confirm the structure is a compressible vein.
Track the needle tip, not just tissue movement, in short or long axis as you advance.
Confirm flash, then lower the angle and advance several more millimeters before threading the catheter.
Confirm intraluminal position by flushing while imaging; watch for tissue bulging that signals infiltration.
Depth over 1.2 cm predicts failure. If the patient needs reliable access for days, a deep PIV is the wrong device.
indications: Difficult intravenous access where surface veins are unavailable or repeatedly fail
Need for reliable peripheral access before escalating to central access
Patients requiring contrast, medications, or resuscitation without an existing line.
contraindications: An easily visible or palpable suitable vein
Cellulitis, burn, or wound over the intended site
Need for high-flow large-bore central access or vesicant/irritant infusions that warrant central access
Extremity that should be avoided (e.g., AV fistula side, mastectomy/lymphedema)
anatomy: Common forearm and upper-arm targets include the basilic, brachial, and cephalic veins.
In the medial upper arm, the brachial veins flank the brachial artery and lie near the median nerve — identify all three before puncture.
Veins are compressible and lack a pulsatile, thick wall; arteries are pulsatile and noncompressible.
Deeper veins need a longer catheter. Aim for at least 2.75 cm of catheter inside the vein; depth over 1.2 cm independently predicts early failure.
equipment: high-frequency linear probe for Ultrasound.
Long peripheral IV catheter chosen from the measured depth: about 4.8 cm at 1 cm deep, about 6.3 cm at 1.5 cm deep.
Single-use gel
Skin antiseptic (chlorhexidine)
Tourniquet
Saline flush and extension set
Securement dressing and tape
Sharps container
positioning: Position the arm on a flat, supported surface with the site facing up.
Apply a tourniquet proximally to distend the target vein.
Place the ultrasound screen directly in your line of sight beyond the puncture site.
Sit or stand so your hand, the probe, and the screen form a comfortable straight line.
steps: Survey the extremity with ultrasound; find a compressible vein with a straight segment and measure its depth before choosing the catheter.
Distinguish the vein from adjacent artery and nerve.
Pick the catheter from that measurement: enough length for the angled skin-to-vein path plus at least 2.75 cm sitting inside the vein.
Clean the skin and prepare a long catheter and flush.
Center the vein on the screen in short axis.
Insert the catheter at roughly 30-45 degrees, advancing while keeping the needle tip in view.
On flash, lower the angle and advance 2-4 mm further.
Thread the catheter off the needle into the vein while stabilizing the hub.
Release the tourniquet, withdraw the needle into the safety device, and attach the extension set.
Aspirate and flush while imaging; confirm intraluminal flow without tissue bulging.
Secure with a clear dressing.
ultrasound: Short-axis is easiest for centering; long-axis confirms the catheter lies within the lumen.
Compress to confirm the target is a vein, not an artery, before puncture.
Keep the needle tip in view at all times; advance the probe ahead to relocate a lost tip.
After threading, image the catheter within the vein and watch the flush for intraluminal turbulence rather than tissue expansion.
confirmation: Blood flash and smooth catheter threading
Catheter visualized within the vein lumen on ultrasound
Flushes easily without resistance or tissue bulging
No pulsatile bleeding
Secured with a clear dressing and dated
troubleshooting: Flash but catheter will not thread: the tip is against a wall or only the needle entered — lower the angle, advance slightly, and re-confirm tip position.
Lost needle tip: stop advancing; slide the probe forward to find the tip before moving the needle.
Vein rolls or collapses: reduce probe pressure, reposition, or choose a better-supported segment.
Swelling or resistance on flush: infiltration — stop, remove, hold pressure, and select a new site.
Bright pulsatile blood: arterial puncture — remove, hold firm pressure, and reassess.
complications: Infiltration or extravasation, especially with short catheters in deep veins; a deep upper-arm site under a drape or in a scanner bore goes unwitnessed until the volume is large.
Nerve irritation or injury near the brachial bundle
aftercare: Reassess the site for infiltration before and during infusions, particularly with deeper placements.
Document catheter length and depth.
Replace per local dwell-time policy and remove when no longer needed.
Educate the patient to report swelling, pain, or leakage at the site.
documentation: Ultrasound-guided peripheral IV for difficult access.
Vein compressible and non-pulsatile; adjacent artery and nerve identified and avoided.
Long catheter; intraluminal position confirmed by ultrasound and flush.
Site secured with a clear dressing and labeled.
No immediate evidence of arterial puncture, infiltration, or nerve injury.
seniorPearls: Match catheter length to measured depth, not habit.
If you cannot keep the needle tip on screen, fan or slide the probe and find it before advancing.
The medial upper arm is rich in arteries and nerves - confirm the structure is a vein before puncture.
references: CDC. Use Only Sterile Ultrasound Gel for Percutaneous Procedures. 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/healthcare-associated-infections/bulletins/outbreak-ultrasound-gel.html

Society of Hospital Medicine. Recommendations on the Use of Ultrasound Guidance for Central and Peripheral Vascular Access in Adults. J Hosp Med. 2019;14:E1-E22. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10193861/
Association of Anaesthetists. Safe Vascular Access 2025. Anaesthesia. 2025. https://associationofanaesthetists-publications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/anae.16727
Pandurangadu AV et al. Ultrasound-guided intravenous catheter survival impacted by amount of catheter residing in the vein. Emerg Med J. 2018;35(9):550-555. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30021833/
Fields JM et al. Predictors of ultrasound-guided peripheral intravenous catheter failure. Am J Emerg Med. 2022;60:1-6. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36113061/
American College of Radiology. ACR Manual on Contrast Media. 2024 edition with 2025 chapter updates. https://cs.acr.org/-/media/ACR/Files/Clinical-Resources/Contrast_Media.pdf

visualAssets.title: Short-axis probe positioning
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe perpendicular to the target vein. Vein appears as a round anechoic compressible structure. Artery is pulsatile and non-compressible.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Compress to distinguish vein from artery before needle entry.

visualAssets.title: Needle tip visualization
visualAssets.subtitle: Track the needle tip as a hyperechoic dot entering the vein lumen. Tenting of the anterior wall confirms contact. Flash in the catheter hub confirms intraluminal position.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Always visualize the needle tip, not just the shaft. Shaft visualization can be deceptive about true tip location.

shiftMode: This is a vision-saving, time-critical procedure — do not wait for ophthalmology or imaging if the diagnosis is clear.
Diagnose clinically: acute orbital compartment syndrome with a tense, proptotic eye, decreased vision/APD, raised intraocular pressure, and pain after trauma or retrobulbar hemorrhage.
The goal is to release the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon.
Anesthetize and clamp the lateral canthus to reduce bleeding, then cut horizontally to the orbital rim.
Strum for the inferior crus and cut it; the lower lid should swing free and the globe should soften.
Reassess intraocular pressure and proptosis; if still tense, release the superior crus as well.
Do not let lack of an ophthalmologist delay the release in a clear orbital compartment syndrome.
indications: Acute orbital compartment syndrome with threat to vision
Markedly raised intraocular pressure with a tense, proptotic globe and an afferent pupillary defect
Progressive vision loss with orbital tension after facial/orbital trauma or surgery
contraindications: Suspected globe rupture - manipulating the orbit can extrude intraocular contents
No evidence of orbital compartment syndrome
An alternative, immediately treatable cause of the findings that does not involve orbital pressure
anatomy: The lateral canthal tendon anchors the eyelids to the orbital rim and has a superior and an inferior crus.
Cantholysis of the inferior crus releases the lower lid and decompresses the orbit
The orbital septum and retrobulbar space hold the hemorrhage that raises pressure on the optic nerve and its blood supply.
The lacrimal apparatus sits medially; the lateral approach avoids it. Aim toward the lateral orbital rim, away from the globe.
equipment: Local anesthetic with epinephrine: 1-2 mL of 1% lidocaine with epinephrine, a small syringe, and a 25-27G needle
Straight hemostat
Blunt-tipped scissors. Not iris or sharp straight scissors.
Toothed forceps
Gauze and saline for hemostasis and visualization
Tonometer to measure intraocular pressure if available
Eye protection/sterile gloves
Good lighting or headlamp
positioning: Patient supine with the head stabilized and the affected eye fully accessible.
Optimize lighting directly on the lateral canthus.
Have an assistant help retract the lids and manage bleeding if available.
Position yourself at the side of the affected eye for a horizontal lateral approach.
steps: Confirm orbital compartment syndrome clinically and exclude obvious globe rupture.
Infiltrate local anesthetic with epinephrine into the lateral canthus toward the lateral orbital rim.
Clamp the lateral canthus horizontally with a hemostat for 1-2 minutes to crush tissue and reduce bleeding.
Remove the hemostat and make a horizontal canthotomy incision through the crushed tissue to the lateral orbital rim (about 1-2 cm).
Pull the lower lid outward and downward with forceps to put the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon on tension.

Strum and identify the taut inferior crus, then cut it with the blunt scissors directed toward the orbital rim - inferiorly and slightly posteriorly, away from the globe. The lower lid should release and the globe soften.
Confirm the inferior release is complete before anything else. The lid should swing freely away from the globe; if it does not, there is still tendon to cut - cut it rather than moving superior.
Reassess: intraocular pressure, visual acuity or at least light perception, the pupil, and orbital tension.

Release the superior crus only if all of these are true after a complete inferior cantholysis:
- the orbit is still tense
- the intraocular pressure is still raised
- vision or the pupil has not improved.
Control bleeding with gentle pressure and arrange emergent ophthalmology evaluation.
confirmation: Lower lid swings free after inferior cantholysis
Globe is visibly softer and proptosis reduced
Measured intraocular pressure has fallen toward normal if a tonometer is available
Improvement (or halted deterioration) in vision and pupillary findings
Hemostasis achieved at the canthotomy site
troubleshooting: No softening after the incision: the canthotomy cut alone is insufficient - perform the cantholysis.
Still tense after inferior cantholysis: confirm the release was complete before going superior.
Cannot identify the crus: pull the lid on tension and strum for the taut band toward the orbital rim before cutting.
Brisk bleeding obscuring the field: apply gentle pressure and use the pre-incision hemostat clamp to limit it.
Suspect globe rupture mid-procedure: stop manipulating the globe and get emergent ophthalmology.
complications: Iatrogenic globe injury if the cut strays toward the globe
Incomplete decompression from canthotomy without cantholysis
Scarring or lid malposition after repair
Failure to restore vision if decompression is delayed
Superior release adds lacrimal artery and gland risk.
aftercare: Arrange emergent ophthalmology evaluation and definitive management.
Continue measures to lower intraocular pressure per ophthalmology guidance.
Serially reassess vision, pupil, and orbital tension until specialist care assumes the patient.
Document the time of decompression relative to symptom onset.
documentation: Lateral canthotomy and inferior (with or without superior) cantholysis performed for acute orbital compartment syndrome.
Clinical findings: proptosis, intraocular pressure with the value, visual acuity or best available assessment, and pupillary findings including relative afferent pupillary defect.
Both eyes documented - the unaffected eye is the baseline.
Vision or pupil not assessable (intubated, obtunded, lids too swollen) recorded as not testable, not left blank.
Globe rupture not suspected prior to the procedure.
Inferior crus released with resultant lid release and globe softening; whether the superior crus was released, and the findings that justified it.
Post-procedure intraocular pressure, vision, and pupillary findings recorded, with the times.
Emergent ophthalmology consultation arranged; time from onset to decompression documented.
seniorPearls: The canthotomy is the approach; the cantholysis is the treatment. Cutting skin without releasing the crus does nothing for the pressure.
Cut now, consult after. Sight is lost quickly when there is optic nerve ischemia.
If the globe might be ruptured, stop - decompression can extrude a salvageable eye.
references: U.S. Joint Trauma System. Eye Trauma: Initial Care Clinical Practice Guideline. 2021. https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Eye_Trauma_Initial_Care_01_Jun_2021_ID03.pdf
American Academy of Ophthalmology EyeWiki. Orbital Compartment Syndrome. https://eyewiki.aao.org/Orbital_Compartment_Syndrome

shiftMode: Confirm anterior dislocation; document neurovascular status - especially axillary nerve sensation over the deltoid - before and after.
Neurovascular compromise means reduce sooner, not wait - reduction fixes it. Call the specialist in parallel, not first.

Dislocation with axillary nerve deficit
Dislocation with a pulseless or ischemic limb - reduce urgently while vascular surgery is called
Recurrent dislocation appropriate for ED reduction
contraindications: Displaced fracture warranting orthopedic reduction (e.g., certain surgical-neck fractures) - traction can displace the head further
Posterior or inferior dislocation - different, specific approach
Open dislocation - reduce in theater
Unable to safely provide required analgesia/sedation
Neurovascular compromise is not a contraindication - see indications and troubleshooting.

The axillary nerve wraps the surgical neck of the humerus and is the most commonly injured nerve - test deltoid sensation and function.

Procedural sedation monitoring and supplies if used, per that card (pulse oximetry, capnography, oxygen, airway kit)

Sheet for counter-traction (traction technique)

steps: Confirm the diagnosis; document neurovascular exam including axillary nerve function.

Intra-articular block: sterile prep, lateral or posterior approach into the joint, aspirate, inject. 20 mL of 1% lidocaine is 200 mg - check the dose calculator on this card before adding any other local anesthetic.
First-line low-force technique: scapular manipulation, Cunningham, or external rotation.
Slow, steady force; let the muscles relax over time.
Feel or watch for the humeral head relocating into the glenoid.
If unsuccessful: optimize analgesia and switch technique rather than escalate force abruptly.
Confirm clinically (contour, motion); recheck neurovascular status.
Post-reduction imaging to confirm position and assess for fracture.
Sling/immobilizer; orthopedic follow-up.
ultrasound: Posterior approach confirms dislocation and reduction in real time, before formal films.
Reduces repeat radiographs; guides intra-articular block placement.
confirmation: Humeral head relocated; shoulder contour restored
Improved range of motion, less pain
Intact post-reduction neurovascular exam, including axillary nerve
Imaging: congruent joint, no new fracture
Immobilized; follow-up arranged
troubleshooting: Pulseless or cold limb: reduce urgently, vascular surgery in parallel. Recheck the pulse as soon as the head relocates.
Pulse not back after reduction: treat as arterial injury until imaging excludes it. Axillary artery injury is commonest in the elderly.
Reduction failing: add an intra-articular block or sedation, and switch technique.
Repeated failure: reassess for fracture or another dislocation type; involve orthopedics.
New deficit after reduction: document; urgent orthopedic/neuro evaluation. A deficit present before and unchanged after is usually an axillary nerve traction injury and usually recovers.
Fracture on the pre-reduction film: weigh technique choice; consult orthopedics.
Severe pain limiting any technique: optimize analgesia before continuing; do not force traction.
complications: Rotator cuff injury, especially in older patients
Sedation-related complications when procedural sedation is used
aftercare: Sling or immobilizer for one to three weeks; shorter is generally preferred.
First dislocation under about 25: high recurrence; orthopedic assessment for stabilization.
Over about 40: suspect a rotator cuff tear and arrange assessment; treat persistent weakness as a cuff tear until examined.
Early range of motion within the limits orthopedics set.
Analgesia; avoid abduction with external rotation.
Orthopedic follow-up.
Return precautions: numbness, weakness, worsening pain, a cold or pale hand, recurrent dislocation.
documentation: Anterior shoulder dislocation confirmed; pre-reduction neurovascular exam documented (axillary nerve sensation, deltoid function, distal pulse).
Any deficit present before reduction recorded as pre-existing, with the time.
Analgesia/sedation method; intra-articular agent, concentration, and volume if used.
Technique(s) and number of attempts.
Reduction confirmed clinically and on post-reduction imaging.
Post-reduction neurovascular exam intact, or deficits compared with the pre-reduction exam.
Immobilization and orthopedic follow-up.
seniorPearls: Most failed reductions are failed analgesia. Relax the patient first.
Nerve deficit: reduce without delay; the nerve is stretched over the displaced humeral head.
High-traction methods add fracture and soft-tissue risk.

Progressive analgesia in the femoral distribution over the expected onset time

Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.

Continue multimodal analgesia and reassess pain regularly.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Motor block means the limb cannot bear weight - a fall risk in older patients. Say so to the patient and at handover.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.

Side and level, named unambiguously.

Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.

shiftMode: Signs of life, any one of: palpable pulse, measurable blood pressure, spontaneous respiratory effort, pupillary reaction, spontaneous or purposeful movement, organized cardiac electrical activity. None of the six at any point since injury: do not open.
CPR-duration windows (WTA 2024): under 15 minutes for penetrating trauma, under 10 minutes for blunt. Blunt arrest without signs of life: not indicated at any duration.
Theater, surgeon, and massive transfusion activated before the incision — do not open without a surgical destination.
Goals, in order: release tamponade, control intrathoracic hemorrhage, internal cardiac massage, cross-clamp the descending aorta for subdiaphragmatic bleeding.
Left anterolateral thoracotomy at the 4th/5th intercostal space; extend across the sternum (clamshell) for right-sided or wider access.
Open the pericardium longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve.
indications: Penetrating thoracic trauma, signs of life at some point since injury, CPR under 15 minutes - the strongest indication
Penetrating extrathoracic trauma, same window: consider; lower yield, source may be abdominal
Blunt trauma arrest with signs of life and CPR under 10 minutes
Traumatic arrest with tamponade on ultrasound and a correctable source
Exsanguinating intrathoracic hemorrhage, aortic cross-clamp as a bridge to theater
Exsanguinating abdominopelvic hemorrhage: laparotomy, or Zone 1 REBOA where available and on the local pathway - not thoracotomy
contraindications: Blunt trauma arrest with no signs of life: survival effectively zero; not indicated at any CPR duration.
No signs of life at any point since injury, for any mechanism
CPR beyond 15 minutes for penetrating or 10 minutes for blunt trauma
No operating theater, surgeon, or blood available
Injuries clearly incompatible with survival, including devastating head injury
Adult criteria only. Use the pediatric trauma pathway for children.
anatomy: Left anterolateral approach at the 4th-5th intercostal space runs along the rib's superior margin, clear of the neurovascular bundle.
The phrenic nerve runs along the lateral pericardium.
The descending aorta lies against the spine. The esophagus lies immediately anterior to it and is the structure most often clamped by mistake - an orogastric tube makes it identifiable by feel.
Clamshell exposes both pleural cavities and the heart.
Crossing the sternum divides both internal mammary arteries: little bleeding without circulation, brisk once it returns - ligate them.
equipment: Thoracotomy/clamshell tray: scalpel, Mayo scissors, rib spreader (Finochietto retractor)
Sternal-division instrument: heavy trauma shears, Lebsche knife, or Gigli saw - know which your tray has.
Vascular clamps, aortic and DeBakey-type
Toothed forceps and large hemostats
Internal defibrillator paddles, confirmed to connect to your defibrillator - paddle and connector generations are not interchangeable
Suction and plenty of gauze/laparotomy pads
Massive transfusion products and rapid infuser
Orogastric tube, to identify the esophagus before clamping the aorta
Foley catheter or sutures for temporary cardiac wound control; skin stapler for rapid closure
Gloves, gowns, eye protection, and face shields for the whole team
positioning: Supine, left arm raised or abducted.
Operate from the patient's left.
Airway management and resuscitation continue.
Prep quickly.
steps: Confirm the criteria by the numbers; activate trauma surgery, massive transfusion, and theater.
Left anterolateral incision at the 4th-5th intercostal space along the superior rib margin, from the sternal edge to the table.
Divide intercostals and enter the pleura; rib spreader handle toward the axilla, out of the field.
Clamshell across the sternum for right-sided injury or wider exposure; find and ligate both internal mammary arteries.
Open the pericardium longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve; evacuate clot. A tamponaded pericardium is tense and hard to pinch up - grasp and incise it.
Cardiac wounds: finger pressure first, then Foley balloon, staples, or sutures. Do not tie a suture around a coronary artery.

Two-handed internal cardiac massage. Internal defibrillation only for a shockable rhythm, at low internal-paddle energy - commonly about 10-20 J, confirmed against your paddle and defibrillator instructions.

Cross-clamp the descending aorta only for subdiaphragmatic bleeding or to redirect circulation to heart and brain. Retract the left lung anteriorly, open the posterior pleura, find the aorta against the spine with the esophagus anterior to it, and clamp under direct vision.
Call the clamp time aloud on application and every five minutes. Everything below the clamp is ischemic; expect a second resuscitation on release.
Control intrathoracic bleeding; continue blood product resuscitation.
Endpoint: no organized cardiac activity after tamponade release, hemorrhage control, and an aortic clamp. Stop there.
Circulation restored: straight to the operating room for definitive repair.
ultrasound: Can identify tamponade before or around the arrest and support the decision to proceed.
Cardiac standstill is not a free-standing reason to stop.
PEA with no signs of life: absent wall motion on a technically adequate view supports termination.
In a patient with signs of life it changes nothing.
Do not delay a clearly indicated thoracotomy for a scan or repeat a scan to postpone the decision.
confirmation: Pericardium opened and tamponade relieved if present
Cardiac or great-vessel bleeding controlled
Aorta clamped under direct vision with the esophagus identified, clamp time recorded, and central perfusion improved
Return of organized cardiac activity or perfusing rhythm as the resuscitation endpoint
Patient moving to definitive operative care without delay
troubleshooting: Cannot get exposure: the incision is too short or too high. Extend it to the table and across the sternum.
No cardiac wound found after opening the pericardium: inspect the posterior surface and great vessels; lift the heart carefully.
Ongoing massive hemorrhage from the chest: pack, control the source, and cross-clamp the aorta while transfusing.
Sudden brisk bleeding after return of circulation in a clamshell: the internal mammary arteries. Look at the sternal edges first.
Clamp on, no change after a few minutes: check the clamp first - probably on the esophagus (check by feel against the orogastric tube) - or the bleeding is above it.
complications: Iatrogenic injury to the heart, lung, phrenic nerve, or great vessels
Esophageal injury from clamping the wrong posterior structure
Internal mammary bleeding after clamshell, unmasked by return of circulation
Coronary or aortic injury during clamping
Distal ischemia below the clamp, and the reperfusion physiology when it comes off
Inadequate exposure leading to missed injury
Team blood-borne exposure during a rapid open procedure
Very high mortality given the underlying physiology
aftercare: Release the aortic clamp as early as tolerated, and announce it - reperfusion drops the pressure and returns the products of ischemia to the circulation.
Hand clamp on and off times to the surgical team explicitly.
Continue massive transfusion; correct coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia.
Debrief the team; address occupational exposures.
documentation: Resuscitative thoracotomy for [penetrating/blunt] trauma arrest meeting local criteria.
Mechanism, CPR duration in minutes, and which signs of life were present and when, named individually.
Procedure: thoracotomy with or without clamshell, pericardiotomy, hemorrhage control, aortic cross-clamp as applicable.
Aortic clamp application and release times.
Intraoperative findings and interventions.
Resuscitation endpoint and disposition (OR vs. termination) against the criteria used.
Team exposures and debrief.
seniorPearls: Apply the criteria before opening.
Tamponade release is often the highest-yield action.
The commonest technical failure is a small incision. Cut from the sternum to the table.
All of this is temporizing; to theater as soon as there is circulation.

visualAssets.title: Pericardiotomy & phrenic nerve
visualAssets.subtitle: Anterolateral incision, entry at the rib margin, and a longitudinal pericardial opening anterior to the phrenic nerve.
visualAssets.caption: Supine male chest from above, patient's left on the right: incision in the 4th-5th intercostal space on the upper edge of the rib below; window shows the pericardium opened longitudinally, anterior to the phrenic nerve.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Open the pericardium longitudinally and anterior to the phrenic nerve.

shiftMode: Tibia is the default site when unsure. Humerus flows faster and reaches central circulation sooner in arrest, but is mis-sited more often and dislodges during CPR.
Responsive patient: lidocaine first, then flush.
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free: 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg ceiling. Use the calculator — a flat adult dose can be many times the correct dose for an infant.
Nearly all IV medications and fluids can be given IO. Pressure bag or push-pull syringe for rapid infusion.
Aim to remove within 24 hours; transition to definitive IV access once stable.
indications: Failed or impossible peripheral IV access, emergent
Cardiac arrest when IV access has failed or is not feasible - adult guidance attempts IV first
Critically ill or injured patient requiring immediate vascular access
Pediatric resuscitation when IV access not rapidly obtained
Severe dehydration with vascular collapse
contraindications: Fracture in the target bone
Attempted or established IO access in the target bone within the past 48 hours
Overlying infection or burn at insertion site
Prosthetic joint or hardware at target site
Conditions with fragile bone (relative: osteogenesis imperfecta, severe osteoporosis)
Excessive tissue over the site, or landmarks that cannot be identified
anatomy: Proximal tibia: flat anteromedial surface, 1-2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity.
Proximal humerus: greater tubercle. Insert at 45 degrees to the anterior plane aimed posteromedially - not 90 degrees.
Distal tibia: medial malleolus, 1-2 cm proximal to the most prominent point.
Pediatrics: proximal tibia preferred.
equipment: EZ-IO driver with needle sets: 15 mm (3-39 kg), 25 mm (40 kg and above), 45 mm (excess tissue, and the proximal humerus in most adults)
Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine
Gloves, eye protection
Normal saline flush syringes: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child
Lidocaine 2%, preservative-free and epinephrine-free, for responsive patients
Extension tubing and IV setup
Pressure bag
Stabilizer/dressing
Sharps container
positioning: Proximal tibia: leg slightly externally rotated, small towel roll behind the knee.
Proximal humerus: arm adducted, hand on abdomen to internally rotate.
steps: Identify the site; confirm no contraindication in that limb.
Prep with antiseptic.
Stabilize the limb without placing your hand behind the target bone.
Needle by tissue depth, not age: 15 mm for 3-39 kg, 25 mm for 40 kg and above, 45 mm for excess tissue and the proximal humerus in most adults.
Touch the tip to bone. At least the 5 mm mark must be visible above the skin before you drill; if not, use a longer needle.
Trajectory: 90 degrees to bone at the tibia and distal femur; 45 degrees to the anterior plane, aimed posteromedially, at the proximal humerus.
Drill to loss of resistance (a subtle give or pop).
Remove the trocar, attach a syringe, aspirate.

Responsive patient: preservative-free, epinephrine-free lidocaine 2% at the weight-based dose on the max-dose card, slowly over about 120 seconds. Do not flush first - flush distension of the marrow is the pain the lidocaine prevents.
Dwell about 60 seconds, then flush: 5-10 mL normal saline in adults, 2-5 mL in infants and children.
Connect extension set and IV tubing; pressure bag for rapid infusion.
Secure with stabilizer dressing.
Document time of insertion, site, confirmation method, and complications.
confirmation: Needle stands upright without support
Loss of resistance on drilling
Marrow aspirate - absence does not rule out placement
Flush flows freely without subcutaneous swelling
Medications and fluids infuse without extravasation
troubleshooting: No flow: confirm trocar removed, recheck position, attempt gentle flush. Extravasation: remove, use a different bone.
Needle loose or wobbly: likely through-and-through cortex penetration. Remove; use a different site.
Pain in a responsive patient: weight-based lidocaine over 120 seconds and the 60-second dwell before flushing. About half the initial dose can be repeated if pain recurs.
Swelling at site: extravasation from malposition. Remove needle, compress, reassess compartment.
Lidocaine without effect in a small child: the extension set's dead space can hold most of the dose - prime it, or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
complications: Osteomyelitis (rare, risk increases if left in >24 hours)
Fracture (rare, more common with manual devices in pediatrics)
Pain during infusion in conscious patients
aftercare: Transition to peripheral or central IV access as soon as feasible.
Aim to remove within 24 hours. Labelling permits up to 48 hours in selected patients aged 12 and over with no alternative access - do not pull a patient's only access to meet a deadline.
Document removal time and any complications.
Watch the site for infection, swelling, or compartment syndrome.
documentation: IO access at [site] using [device] for [indication].
Verbal/implied consent in emergent setting.
Site prepped, needle inserted with loss of resistance confirmed.
Flushed with [volume] normal saline without extravasation.
IO lidocaine before infusion (if conscious).
Procedure tolerated; removal within 24 hours and transition to definitive access.
seniorPearls: Crashing patient, no peripheral line in 90 seconds: drill.
Lidocaine before the flush; three minutes including the dwell.
Peds: through-and-through risk. Use the correct needle length and stop at loss of resistance.
Trust the 5 mm mark over the weight chart: it measures how much needle is left after the tissue.
references: Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO intraosseous vascular access procedure template, document MCI-2019-0395. https://www.teleflex.com/global/clinical-resources/documents/MCI-2019-0395_Arrow_EZ-IO_Intraosseous_Procedure_Template_LR.pdf

Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO procedure competency template, MC-000270 rev 2c. 2021. https://www.teleflex.com/usa/en/clinical-resources/ez-io/documents/EM_IOS_EZIO%20Procedure-Competency-Template_MC-000270_rev2c.pdf
Teleflex. Arrow EZ-IO indications and contraindications data sheet. https://go.teleflex.com/EZUI-Procedure-Tray-Data-Sheet.html

American Heart Association. 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC: Adult Advanced Life Support, vascular access. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support

visualAssets.title: Proximal tibia insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Palpate the tibial tuberosity. Move 1-2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity, onto the flat anteromedial tibial surface. This is the insertion point. Needle at 90 degrees to the bone.
visualAssets.caption: Right knee from the front, lateral on the left: target 1-2 cm distal and medial to the tibial tuberosity, on the flat anteromedial surface.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Do not place your hand behind the limb during drilling.

visualAssets.title: Proximal humerus insertion site
visualAssets.subtitle: Arm adducted, hand on abdomen (internal rotation). Palpate the greater tubercle — the most prominent lateral bony point of the shoulder. Needle at 45 degrees to the anterior plane, aimed posteromedially - not 90 degrees.
visualAssets.caption: Right shoulder from the front, lateral on the left, hand on the abdomen: target the greater tubercle. Inset from the head of the bed: needle 45 degrees to the anterior plane, aimed posteromedially.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Humeral IO flows faster than tibial in adults. Secure well — humeral IOs dislodge more easily.

agents.note: Preservative-free and epinephrine-free only. Adults are given 40 mg initially regardless of weight; infants and children get 0.5 mg/kg to a 40 mg maximum, which is the figure computed here.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
caveats: This is the dose to give, not a range to stay under.
At pediatric volumes the extension set's dead space can hold most of the dose. Prime the set or follow with the age-appropriate flush.
monitoring: Infuse slowly over about 120 seconds, then allow a 60-second dwell before flushing.
Flush volume is age-specific: 5-10 mL adult, 2-5 mL infant or child.
Reassess the site and the whole limb for extravasation before every infusion.

shiftMode: Superolateral approach is most common; medial is the alternative.
Always send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
Tap before antibiotics if the patient can wait a few minutes. If septic or in shock: antibiotics first (blood cultures first), tap after - document the sample as post-antibiotic.
Ultrasound improves success, especially in obesity or small effusions.
indications: Acute monoarticular arthritis to evaluate for septic joint
Crystal arthropathy workup (gout, pseudogout)
Hemarthrosis evaluation
Symptomatic relief of tense effusion
Traumatic effusion with concern for intra-articular fracture or lipohemarthrosis
contraindications: Cellulitis or skin infection at the insertion site
Significant coagulopathy (relative; weigh against a suspected septic joint)
Prosthetic joint (consult orthopedics before tapping)
Patient refusal
anatomy: Superolateral: 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superolateral pole of the patella, directed medially beneath the patella into the suprapatellar recess.
Medial: midpoint of the patella on the medial side, directed posterolaterally.
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the joint - an alternative US-guided target.
Avoid the popliteal fossa (neurovascular structures).
equipment: Sterile gloves and drape
Chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine
5 mL of 1% lidocaine, 25G needle for the skin wheal
18G needle and 20-60 mL syringe

Sterile containers for the primary samples; remaining fluid into blood culture bottles. Confirm tube colors, and whether the lab accepts a culture bottle as the primary specimen, with the lab that runs it.
Sterile dressing
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe (if available)
Hemostat (optional, for syringe exchange)
positioning: Supine, knee flexed 15-20 degrees over a rolled towel.
Quadriceps relaxed; patella mobile.
steps: Confirm indication; consent.
Knee in slight flexion; identify landmarks or use ultrasound.
Sterile antiseptic prep.
Anesthetize skin and subcutaneous tissue down to the capsule.
Insert the 18G needle at the chosen approach, aspirating gently as you advance.
Aspirate. With a large syringe, a hemostat stabilizes the needle during syringe exchange.
Remove as much fluid as is clinically appropriate.
Remove the needle; sterile dressing.
Send fluid for cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe, longitudinal over the suprapatellar recess.
Anechoic collection confirms effusion; complex or echogenic fluid may suggest infection or hemorrhage.
In-plane needle guidance.
Most useful in obesity or an equivocal exam.
confirmation: Synovial fluid aspirated
Effusion clinically reduced
Fluid sent for studies
troubleshooting: Dry tap: reposition, use ultrasound; consider a small or loculated effusion.
Bloody aspirate: hemarthrosis or traumatic tap - send it. Lipohemarthrosis on gross inspection suggests intra-articular fracture.
Needle hits bone: redirect slightly.
Quadriceps will not relax: coach, ensure adequate local anesthesia.
complications: Iatrogenic septic arthritis (rare with sterile technique)
aftercare: Return for increasing pain, redness, warmth, fever.
Keep the dressing clean and dry for 24 hours.
Follow up culture and crystal results.
Suspected septic arthritis: treat and admit without waiting for results. In sepsis or septic shock, empiric antibiotics go immediately, before or without the aspirate.
documentation: Knee arthrocentesis, [side] knee, for [indication].
Consent obtained.
Sterile prep; local anesthesia.
Aspirated [volume] mL of [appearance] fluid via [approach].
Sent for cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystal analysis.
No immediate complication.
Sterile dressing applied.
seniorPearls: Hot swollen joint and unsure whether to tap: tap it.
Clear straw-colored fluid does not rule out infection; send the labs.

No synovial white cell count rules septic arthritis in or out. Above 50,000 raises the probability without confirming it; below 50,000 does not exclude it, particularly early, in the immunocompromised, and in prosthetic joints.
Crystals do not exclude infection; gout and a septic joint can coexist in the same knee.
references: European Bone and Joint Infection Society. Guideline for the management of septic arthritis in native joints (SANJO). J Bone Jt Infect. 2023;8(1):29-37. https://doi.org/10.5194/jbji-8-29-2023
Food and Drug Administration. Xylocaine and Xylocaine with epinephrine prescribing information. 2024. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2024/006488Orig1s100lbl.pdf
Confirm specimen containers and order with the laboratory that will process them, and verify institutional policy on anticoagulation and prosthetic joint aspiration.

visualAssets.title: Superolateral approach
visualAssets.subtitle: 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the superolateral pole of the patella. Direct the needle medially beneath the patella into the suprapatellar recess, posterior and slightly inferior.
visualAssets.caption: Right knee from the front, lateral on the left: enter 1 cm superior and 1 cm lateral to the patella's superolateral pole, aiming medially under the patella.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: Avoid posterior approach (popliteal neurovascular bundle).

visualAssets.title: Suprapatellar recess ultrasound
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe placed longitudinally over the suprapatellar recess. Anechoic fluid between the quadriceps tendon and femur confirms effusion.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Most anterior epistaxis is from Kiesselbach plexus on the septum.
Start with direct pressure: pinch the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes continuously.
If a single bleeding point is visible, silver nitrate cautery may stop the bleed without packing.
If packing is needed, Rapid Rhino or Merocel sponge are first-line devices.
Always check vitals and hemodynamic stability. Posterior bleeds and anticoagulated patients can hemorrhage.
Patients discharged with packing need ENT follow-up for removal in 48-72 hours.
indications: Anterior epistaxis uncontrolled by direct pressure
Visible anterior bleeding source amenable to packing
Recurrent epistaxis requiring temporizing control
Post-cautery reinforcement when bleeding recurs
contraindications: Suspected posterior epistaxis (pack both if unavoidable, but involve ENT early)
Suspected nasal fracture with CSF leak
Severe midface trauma requiring operative management
anatomy: Kiesselbach plexus: anterior septum, the most common source of anterior epistaxis.
Supplied by branches of anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, superior labial, and greater palatine arteries.
The nasal cavity narrows posteriorly. Packing must fill the anterior space to tamponade the vessel.
Direct packing along the nasal floor, not upward toward the cribriform plate.
equipment: Personal protective equipment (gown, gloves, face shield)
Headlamp or bright light source
Nasal speculum
Suction with Frazier tip
Topical vasoconstrictor (oxymetazoline spray or phenylephrine-soaked pledgets)

Topical anesthetic: 4% lidocaine on cotton pledgets - 40 mg per milliliter. Nasal mucosa absorbs close to intravenous rates; 2-3 mL is 80-120 mg. It counts against the same ceiling as injected local anesthetic, so do not keep re-soaking pledgets to hold the field.
Silver nitrate sticks (for cautery if appropriate)
Nasal packing device: Rapid Rhino, Merocel sponge, or ribbon gauze with petroleum jelly
Resorbable packing for patients with a bleeding disorder or on antithrombotic therapy.
Sterile water to activate a Rapid Rhino's hydrocolloid coating, and a separate syringe of air for its cuff. Water outside the pack, air inside; saline goes in neither.
Antibiotic ointment (for gauze packing)
Kidney basin and gauze for blood management
1g Tranexamic acid (TXA) for topical use; injectable solution applied on a pledget or used to soak the pack
positioning: Patient seated upright leaning slightly forward to prevent blood swallowing.
Have the patient blow out clots gently before examination.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets for 10-15 minutes before instrumentation.
steps: Ensure hemodynamic stability. Obtain IV access if significant bleeding or anticoagulation.
Apply PPE.
Have the patient blow out clots. Suction the nasal cavity.
Apply topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic pledgets. Wait 10-15 minutes.
Remove pledgets and inspect with nasal speculum and headlamp to identify bleeding source.
If a single anterior point is identified and bleeding is controlled: apply silver nitrate to the site for 5-10 seconds. Do not cauterize both sides of the septum simultaneously (perforation risk).
If cautery fails or bleeding is diffuse: proceed to nasal packing.

Rapid Rhino: soak the pack in sterile water for at least 30 seconds to activate the hydrocolloid coating, insert along the nasal floor, then inflate the cuff slowly with air only, using the pilot cuff to judge it. Saline or water in the cuff is contrary to the manufacturer's instructions.
Merocel sponge: insert dry sponge along the nasal floor, then hydrate with saline to expand.
Confirm hemostasis. Check for posterior drainage in the oropharynx.
If bilateral packing is placed, monitor for hypoxia in high-risk patients.
confirmation: Active bleeding has stopped
No posterior drainage seen in the oropharynx on inspection
Packing is seated properly and not extruding
Patient hemodynamically stable
troubleshooting: Continued bleeding after packing: ensure packing fills the anterior cavity adequately. May need additional packing or posterior epistaxis management.
Posterior bleed suspected: blood draining in posterior pharynx despite adequate anterior packing. Place posterior balloon or consult ENT urgently.

Patient on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet: local measures first - pressure, vasoconstrictor, cautery, resorbable packing. Reserve reversal or withholding the drug for life-threatening bleeding, and refer that decision to the prescribing team or hematology, jointly with ENT.
Vasovagal during packing: recline patient, maintain airway, resume when stable.
complications: Nasal septal necrosis or pressure injury (if packing too tight or left too long)
Sinusitis or toxic shock syndrome (rare, from prolonged packing)
aftercare: Discharge with packing in place. Arrange ENT follow-up for removal in 48-72 hours.
Antibiotics after packing are not automatic. Toxic shock syndrome after nasal packing is rare, and routine prophylaxis has not been shown to prevent it.
Instruct patient to keep head elevated, avoid straining, nose blowing, and blood thinners if safe to hold.
Return precautions: recurrent heavy bleeding, difficulty breathing, fever, significant swelling.
documentation: Anterior epistaxis managed with [method: cautery / packing device].
Bleeding source identified on [side] anterior septum.
Bleeding-risk factors recorded: anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy with the agent and last dose, known bleeding disorder, liver disease, hypertension.
Topical vasoconstrictor and anesthetic applied, with the agent, concentration, and approximate amount.
[Cautery performed / packing placed]: device, side, whether resorbable, and inflation medium if applicable.
Removal plan documented with the date and who will remove it.
No posterior drainage observed.
Patient hemodynamically stable. Discharged with ENT follow-up arranged and the transition of care recorded.
Return precautions given.
seniorPearls: Fifteen minutes of real continuous pressure stops most anterior bleeds.
Suction, vasoconstrict, and light the field before touching anything.
Do not cauterize both sides of the septum.
Check the oropharynx - a posterior bleed masquerades as anterior packing failure.

Smith+Nephew. RAPID RHINO usage instructions. https://rapidrhino.com/usage-instructions/

AAO-HNSF. Nosebleed guideline research needs. 2020. https://www.entnet.org/resource/cpg-nosebleed-epistaxis-research-needs/ - The benefit and the ideal duration of antibiotic prophylaxis after nasal packing are both identified as unresolved research questions.

Verify institutional policy on antibiotic prophylaxis with nasal packing, and read the instructions for use of the specific pack your department stocks.

Count every pledget against the running total; re-soaking a pledget is a second dose, not a top-up.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.

Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.
