shiftMode: Confirm SYNC is on before every shock.
Unstable = cardiovert now. Stable = rate control, rhythm control, or elective cardioversion.
Instability: hypotension, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain, acute heart failure.
Sedate unless peri-arrest - see the procedural sedation card.
Pulseless VT or VF: defibrillate (SYNC off, max energy).
Initial biphasic energy: atrial fibrillation 200 J, atrial flutter 200 J, narrow-complex SVT 100 J, monomorphic VT with a pulse 100 J.
Manufacturer's recommended energy takes precedence; know your machine's in advance.
If a shock fails, escalate toward the device maximum; do not repeat the same energy.
indications: Unstable tachyarrhythmia with a pulse (SVT, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, monomorphic VT with a pulse)
Elective cardioversion of persistent atrial fibrillation or flutter, once the anticoagulation or imaging pathway is satisfied
Wide complex tachycardia with hemodynamic compromise
contraindications: Pulseless VT or VF: unsynchronized defibrillation
Polymorphic VT: unsynchronized shock at defibrillation energy; the device cannot synchronize to it
Known left atrial or left atrial appendage thrombus - absolute contraindication to elective cardioversion

Elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation lasting 48 hours or longer, or of unknown duration, without either three weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation or transesophageal echo excluding thrombus
Digitalis toxicity (relative; may precipitate refractory VF)
Multifocal atrial tachycardia (will not respond; treat the cause)
Sinus tachycardia (treat the cause)
anatomy: Anterolateral: right parasternal and left lateral chest wall (V5-V6, mid-axillary line).
Anteroposterior: sternum and left infrascapular area; may be superior for atrial fibrillation.
No pad over an implanted device generator: keep at least 8 cm away, prefer anteroposterior, and confirm the separation your device and defibrillator manufacturers state - 8 cm is not universal.
Remove transdermal medication patches from the pad path; a metal-backed patch can arc and burn.
equipment: Defibrillator with SYNC; know its recommended energies and whether it holds SYNC after a shock
Adhesive defibrillation pads (preferred over paddles)
Cardiac monitor with 12-lead ECG
Sedation per the procedural sedation card
Airway equipment at bedside: BVM, oral airway, suction, intubation supplies
Pulse oximetry and continuous waveform capnography
IV access, ideally two sites
Epinephrine, amiodarone, atropine at bedside
Crash cart
positioning: Supine. Good skin contact: shave excess chest hair, dry the skin.
Press pads down over their whole surface, clear of ECG electrodes and medication patches - both cause burns and raise impedance.
Monitor leads connected, rhythm visible.
steps: Identify the rhythm; confirm instability or the elective plan.
12-lead ECG if time permits.
IV access; pulse oximetry, capnography, cardiac monitor.
Airway equipment at bedside.
Apply pads anterolateral or anteroposterior.
Conscious and not peri-arrest: sedate per the procedural sedation card. Confirm depth before charging.
Select the energy for the rhythm, cross-checked against your defibrillator's recommendation. Activate SYNC.
Verify SYNC markers track the R waves.
Announce "Charging" and charge.
Visual and verbal clear: "I am clear, you are clear, everyone is clear."
Deliver the shock; hold the button until the device fires (SYNC may delay).
Assess the rhythm immediately; if unsuccessful, escalate the energy rather than repeat it.
Confirm SYNC on the screen before every shock; whether it persists after a shock is configurable on current Philips and LIFEPAK platforms.
confirmation: Converted to sinus or target rhythm
Hemodynamic improvement (blood pressure, mentation, perfusion)
Repeat 12-lead ECG shows the new rhythm
troubleshooting: Shock does not fire: SYNC waits for an R wave; a rhythm too irregular or amplitude too low may never trigger it. Change lead, increase ECG gain, or defibrillate unsynchronized if deteriorating.
Rhythm unchanged: escalate energy, check pad contact, try anteroposterior.
Patient moves or remembers the shock: sedation failure. Deepen sedation before the next shock unless peri-arrest.
Deteriorates to VF or pulseless VT: unsynchronized defibrillation at max energy immediately.
Post-cardioversion bradycardia: observe; atropine if symptomatic; transcutaneous pacing at bedside.
Recurrence: consider an antiarrhythmic before repeating cardioversion.
complications: Skin burns at pad sites - worse with poor contact, chest hair, or a shock over an ECG electrode or medication patch
Thromboembolism (stroke) if atrial fibrillation is cardioverted without adequate anticoagulation
Implanted pacemaker or ICD damage or reprogramming
aftercare: Monitor until the rhythm is stable and sedation meets the procedural sedation card's discharge criteria. There is no evidence-based universal telemetry duration for cardioversion itself - observation is a local policy decision driven by the arrhythmia, the sedation, and comorbidity.
Repeat 12-lead ECG.
Check pad sites for burns and chest wall discomfort.
Interrogate any pacemaker or ICD - a shock can alter programming or damage the device.

Anticoagulation: at least four weeks of uninterrupted therapeutic anticoagulation for anyone cardioverted from atrial fibrillation or flutter, whatever the pre-procedure duration; then long-term by stroke risk, not by whether the rhythm held.
An unstable patient cardioverted without the pre-procedure pathway still needs the post-procedure anticoagulation.
documentation: Synchronized cardioversion for [rhythm] with [indication].
Pre-procedure rhythm on 12-lead ECG.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter: duration, and the pre-procedure pathway - anticoagulation, imaging, or urgent without either.
Sedation: [agent, dose, route]; adequate depth.
SYNC confirmed. [Energy] J biphasic; device model.
Post-shock rhythm: [rhythm]. Hemodynamics [stable/improved].
No immediate complication.
Post-procedure 12-lead ECG. Monitoring, device interrogation, and anticoagulation plan.
seniorPearls: The first shock is the one most likely to work: give it at the recommended energy, not a lower one.
Anteroposterior is better for atrial fibrillation. If anterolateral fails, switch before escalating energy.
references: American Heart Association. Electrical Cardioversion Algorithm, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines. 2025. https://www.heart.org/-/media/CPR-Files/CPR-Guidelines-Files/2025-Algorithms/Algorithm-ACLS-Electrical-Cardioversion-250514.pdf

American Heart Association. Part 9: Adult Advanced Life Support, 2025 CPR and ECC Guidelines - synchronized cardioversion energy and manufacturer dose deference. 2025. https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-advanced-life-support — AHA states at least 200 J is reasonable for fibrillation and that 200 J may be reasonable for flutter (a stronger recommendation for fibrillation than flutter), replacing the older practice of starting low and climbing since a failed low-energy shock costs the patient another sedation and another shock; AHA also defers to the manufacturer's stated dose, as biphasic waveforms are not interchangeable across devices.
Joglar JA, et al. 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation. Circulation. 2024;149(1):e1-e156. https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001193

Read your defibrillator's operating instructions for its recommended cardioversion energies, SYNC-persistence configuration, and implanted-device clearance. Philips HeartStart Intrepid and Stryker LIFEPAK 15 are examples: https://www.stryker.com/content/dam/stryker/ems/resources/operating-instructions/international/3314911-030_int-eng_lifepak_15_operating_instructions.pdf
Verify institutional cardioversion and sedation protocols.

shiftMode: Needle aspiration, I&D, and abscess tonsillectomy are all effective; aspiration is the usual bedside choice. Follow local ENT preference.
Airway first: decide whether bedside drainage is appropriate at all (contraindications) before choosing a technique.
Needle guard at 1 cm depth (cut syringe sheath or tape).
Aspirate at maximal fluctuance or bulging, usually the superior pole.
Suction ready - these patients aspirate pus.
No pus but high suspicion: CT with contrast or ENT.
indications: Suspected peritonsillar abscess: unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice
Peritonsillar abscess confirmed on imaging or exam
Peritonsillar cellulitis progressing to abscess despite outpatient antibiotics
contraindications: Any airway warning sign: stridor, drooling or inability to handle secretions, respiratory distress, a tripoding or sniffing posture, or hypoxia. Controlled airway plan with ENT or anesthesia; no bedside needle.
Severe sepsis or septic shock: resuscitate, involve ENT and critical care; drain in a monitored setting, not as an unmonitored bedside procedure.
Deep neck space extension: neck swelling, torticollis, trismus out of proportion, pain on neck movement. Image; consult ENT or surgery.
Pulsatile mass or bruit (vascular anomaly): image first
Severe trismus preventing visualization: sedation or operative drainage
Unable to cooperate (relative): procedural sedation, with that card's monitoring
Bedside drainage needs suction, oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment immediately to hand; without them, move to a room that has them.
anatomy: The peritonsillar space lies between the tonsillar capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
The internal carotid artery runs posterolateral, typically 2-2.5 cm from the pharyngeal mucosal surface.
Most PTAs collect at the superior pole, between the anterior tonsillar pillar and the soft palate.
Uvula deviates away from the affected side.
Landmarks: palatine tonsil, anterior and posterior pillars, soft palate.
equipment: Headlamp or good overhead light
Tongue depressor
Topical anesthetic spray; a lidocaine-based topical is the safer default.
Benzocaine (e.g., Cetacaine): one shortest labelled spray, about one second, no repeat. FDA warning for methemoglobinemia, which can be fatal; the mouth and pharynx absorb quickly.
1% lidocaine with epinephrine, 3 mL syringe, 25G needle
18G needle on a 10 mL syringe
Needle guard: tape or cut syringe cap 1 cm from the tip
Yankauer suction, tested before you start
Oxygen, monitoring, and airway equipment in the room
Kidney basin
Culture specimen cup
Methylene blue in the department if benzocaine is used - treats methemoglobinemia; sign is cyanosis not improving with oxygen
positioning: Seated upright, leaning slightly forward.
Light on the oropharynx.
Tongue depressor in the non-dominant hand.
Mouth open maximally; if trismus limits it, topical anesthetic and a gentle approach, or sedation.
steps: Confirm the diagnosis clinically.
Topical spray to the planned site.
Inject 1% lidocaine with epinephrine into the mucosa over the abscess, aspirating first to exclude vascular puncture.
18G needle on the 10 mL syringe, guard at 1 cm from the tip.
Enter at maximal fluctuance - usually the superior pole, at the junction of anterior pillar and soft palate.
Aspirate while advancing slowly, 1 cm only.
Pus: aspirate as much as possible; send for culture.
No pus: redirect slightly inferior or medial; a second attempt at the middle pole may be tried.
No pus after 2-3 attempts: CT for abscess vs cellulitis, or ENT.
Gargle and spit; reassess the oropharynx.
ultrasound: Intraoral endocavitary probe, covered, identifies the collection and its depth.
Transcutaneous submandibular approach for large collections.
Most useful when the exam is equivocal or aspiration was dry.
confirmation: Pus aspirated
Uvular deviation and tonsillar swelling improve
Swallowing and pain improve
Trismus reduced
troubleshooting: Dry tap: different quadrant; image if repeated attempts fail.
Trismus limiting access: topical anesthetic, procedural sedation, or ENT for operative drainage.
Bleeding: gauze pressure, maintain suction; minor mucosal bleeding is usually self-limited. Pulsatile or brisk bleeding: secure the airway, get ENT and vascular help.
Cyanosis or low saturations after benzocaine, not improving with oxygen: methemoglobinemia. Stop the agent, oxygen, co-oximetry level, methylene blue.
Rapid re-accumulation of a large abscess: ENT for incision and drainage or tonsillectomy.
complications: Aspiration of pus into the airway
Internal carotid artery injury (prevented by the depth guard)
aftercare: Amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin; dose and duration per institutional guidelines.
NSAIDs and paracetamol.
Single-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone is the agent studied) is a reasonable adjunct for pain and trismus. Limited, heterogeneous evidence supports one dose, not a multi-day tapering pack.
Watch them drink before discharge.
Oral hydration; soft diet.
ENT follow-up within 2-3 days.
Return precautions: worsening pain, inability to swallow, difficulty breathing, fever, neck swelling.
documentation: Peritonsillar abscess needle aspiration.
Consent obtained.
Topical and local anesthesia, [side] peritonsillar area.
Superior pole; depth guard at 1 cm.
Aspirated [volume] mL of pus; sent for culture.
No complication.
Antibiotics prescribed; ENT follow-up; return precautions.
seniorPearls: Trismus preventing access: do not force the mouth open. Sedate or consult ENT.
Dry first aspiration: confirm the superior pole was tried before stopping.
Symptoms improve markedly within minutes of drainage.
The 1 cm guard is the margin against the internal carotid.
references: Windfuhr JP, et al. Clinical practice guideline: tonsillitis II. Surgical management. Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol. 2016;273(4):989-1009. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00405-016-3904-x — no drainage technique is established as superior; needle aspiration is often preferred at the bedside because it does not require surgical training.

DailyMed. Cetacaine Topical Anesthetic prescribing information, including the methemoglobinemia warning. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=af1773c5-5d5b-4278-b551-30ad2df6d5b5
Chau JKM, et al. Corticosteroids in peritonsillar abscess treatment: a blinded placebo-controlled clinical trial. Laryngoscope. 2014;124(1):97-103. https://doi.org/10.1002/lary.24283
Verify institutional antibiotic guidelines, the topical anaesthetic on your formulary, and ENT referral pathways.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: X-ray finds most glass, metal, gravel, and bone. Small fragments, some glass, and ceramic are missed.
X-ray does not reliably show wood, plastic, or thorns at all. Ultrasound is the bedside tool for those.
Get adequate anesthesia and a bloodless field before starting.
A digital tourniquet must come off — use a device you can't miss, note the time, and check the finger after.
If you cannot find it in a reasonable time or it is near critical structures, stop and refer.
Document what you found, what you removed, and what imaging showed. If retained FB is possible, tell the patient.
Tetanus status and wound infection risk should be addressed at every visit.
indications: Known or suspected retained foreign body in soft tissue
Wound with mechanism suggesting foreign body (glass, wood, metal)
Non-healing wound or recurrent infection suggesting retained material
Patient-reported foreign body sensation
contraindications: Foreign body near major neurovascular structures requiring operative exploration
Deep foreign body not accessible with bedside techniques
Foreign body that is asymptomatic, deeply embedded, and not causing infection (may be observed in select cases)
Inadequate anesthesia or equipment for safe removal
anatomy: Hand and foot foreign bodies are near tendons, nerves, and vessels in tight compartments.
Plantar foot: flexor tendons, digital nerves, and plantar fascia are at risk during deep exploration.
The depth and tissue plane of the foreign body dictate the approach.
equipment: Local anesthetic
Syringe and needle for anesthesia (25-27G)
Antiseptic prep
Sterile gloves and drape
Scalpel (#11 or #15 blade)
Hemostats (mosquito and Kelly)
Fine-tipped forceps (splinter forceps or Adson)
Iris scissors
Needle driver
Wound irrigation supplies (saline, 18G angiocath on 30-60 mL syringe)

Digit tourniquet that cannot be forgotten: a brightly colored commercial ring tourniquet, or a glove finger or Penrose secured with a large clamp left hanging outside the drape. Not a rolled glove finger tucked under a dressing.
A clock or timer, and something to write the application time on - the drape, the notes, or the patient's chart
Ultrasound with high-frequency linear probe
Suture material for closure if needed
positioning: Position the affected area for optimal access, lighting, and comfort.
Digit procedures: apply the tourniquet only after the field is prepped, record the time of application out loud and in writing, and leave the device visible outside the drape.
Ensure the patient is comfortable and the field is well-lit.
steps: Obtain history: mechanism, timing, material type, symptoms since injury.
Examine the wound. Assess for signs of infection, neurovascular status distally.
Image the area: X-ray for radiopaque materials, ultrasound for radiolucent objects.
Mark the foreign body location on the skin using imaging guidance if needed.
Anesthetize the area with local or regional block as appropriate.
Prep and drape the wound.
Digits: apply the tourniquet now, record the time, and leave the device visible.
If the foreign body is visible or superficial: extract with forceps.
If deeper: make a small incision over the marked location. Blunt dissect along tissue planes using hemostats.
Use ultrasound in real-time to guide your approach to deeper or radiolucent foreign bodies.
Grasp and remove the foreign body. Inspect it for fragmentation.
Irrigate the wound with normal saline.
Reassess the wound. Obtain post-removal imaging if fragmentation is suspected.
Remove the tourniquet. Record the removal time and the total tourniquet time.
Confirm the digit is perfused: capillary refill and color, compared with the neighbouring finger.
Close the wound if appropriate (clean and recent) Leave contaminated or infected wounds open.
Apply appropriate dressing - and confirm again that the tourniquet is not under it.
ultrasound: High-frequency linear probe (10-15 MHz) provides best resolution for superficial foreign bodies.
Foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures, often with posterior shadowing (glass, metal) or reverberation artifact.
Wood may appear as a hyperechoic linear structure with dirty shadowing.
Scan in two orthogonal planes to localize in 3D.
confirmation: Foreign body visualized and removed intact
Post-removal imaging shows no retained fragments.
Wound irrigated and inspected
Tourniquet removed, removal time recorded, and the digit confirmed pink with normal capillary refill
Neurovascular status intact after removal
troubleshooting: Cannot locate foreign body: reimage with ultrasound, try a different scanning plane, consider CT for deep or small objects. Ultrasound sensitivity falls with depth, small size, and operator inexperience.
Fragmented foreign body: remove what is accessible, image to assess residual, discuss with patient and consider specialist referral.
Significant bleeding during exploration: apply direct pressure, tourniquet for digits, consider specialist referral for deep structures.
Foreign body near nerve or tendon: stop if safe extraction is not possible. Refer to hand surgery or appropriate specialist.
Tourniquet time approaching 20-30 minutes: stop, release, and reassess.
complications: Digital ischemia or amputation from a tourniquet left in place
Excessive tissue damage from prolonged exploration
aftercare: Confirm the tourniquet is off before the patient leaves the room. If a handover happens mid-procedure, the tourniquet is the first thing handed over.
Tetanus: assess the wound as clean-minor or dirty-major and the immunization history separately, and give vaccine, tetanus immune globulin, or both accordingly.
Antibiotics for contaminated wounds, bite wounds, or immunocompromised patients
Wound care instructions: keep clean, dressing changes, elevation.
Return precautions: increasing pain, redness, swelling, drainage, fever, or a cold or discolored digit.
If retained FB is possible: disclose to patient, arrange follow-up, document discussion.
documentation: Foreign body removal performed from [location].
Informed consent obtained.
Pre-procedure imaging: [modality] showing [finding], and the limits of that modality for this material noted.
Local anesthesia administered: agent, concentration, and volume. Sterile technique used.
Tourniquet [used/not used]; if used, device type, application time, removal time, and total tourniquet time recorded, with post-removal perfusion documented.
Foreign body identified and removed: [description of object].
Wound irrigated with [volume] normal saline.
Post-procedure neurovascular status intact.
[Wound closed with X / wound left open for healing by secondary intention].
Tetanus status addressed with the vaccine and immune globulin decision recorded. Return precautions and follow-up discussed.
seniorPearls: If you are digging for more than 15 minutes, stop - further exploration only enlarges the wound.
Ultrasound finds much of what X-ray misses and misses things too.
A finger tourniquet turns a bloody mess into a clean field, and costs the finger if it stays on. Write the time down.
references: National Patient Safety Agency. Reducing risks of tourniquets left on after finger and toe surgery. 2010. https://www.cas.mhra.gov.uk/ViewandAcknowledgment/ViewAttachment.aspx?Attachment_id=101035 — documents cases of digital ischemia and loss from tourniquets retained after finger/toe procedures.
American College of Emergency Physicians. Sonoguide: Foreign Body Localization. 2020. https://www.acep.org/sonoguide/procedures/foreign-bodies/
American College of Radiology. Appropriateness Criteria: Suspected Osteomyelitis, Septic Arthritis, or Soft Tissue Infection - 2022 Update. https://acsearch.acr.org/docs/3094201/Narrative/
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus. 2025. https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html
Verify institutional wound management and antibiotic prophylaxis guidelines.

visualAssets.title: Foreign body on ultrasound
visualAssets.subtitle: High-frequency linear probe. Foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures with posterior shadowing (glass, metal) or reverberation artifact. Wood shows dirty shadowing. Scan in two planes.
visualAssets.clinicalWarning: X-ray misses wood, plastic, and thorns. Ultrasound is the bedside tool for radiolucent foreign bodies.

agents.note: Epinephrine raises the ceiling and dries the field. Avoid it in an end-arterial field unless local policy says otherwise.
Higher risk of severe cardiotoxicity than lidocaine or ropivacaine at equivalent doses.

Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.

Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before you start.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

shiftMode: Target: C5-C7 roots between the anterior and middle scalenes.
10-15 mL. Keep the needle tip in view throughout.
Hemidiaphragmatic paresis is volume-dependent; expect it often at this volume. Avoid in severe COPD or respiratory failure.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Shoulder dislocation (pre-reduction)
Proximal humerus fracture
Clavicle fracture (lateral third)
Complex shoulder or upper arm lacerations
contraindications: Contralateral phrenic palsy or severe baseline pulmonary disease (e.g., severe COPD)
Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy: deep block - ASRA applies neuraxial-equivalent timing. Use the drug-specific interval from local policy.
Contralateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy - a second palsy obstructs the airway.
anatomy: C5-C7 roots exit between the anterior and middle scalenes.
The phrenic nerve runs over the anterior scalene.
The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves pass through the middle scalene.
equipment: High-frequency linear transducer
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle: echogenic, short bevel, e.g., 21G or 22G, 50mm
Local anesthetic: 10-15 mL of 0.25% or 0.5% bupivacaine or ropivacaine
Normal saline for hydrodissection (optional but recommended)
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located.
positioning: Supine or semi-recumbent, head turned slightly away from the block side.
Ultrasound machine opposite the provider, in direct line of sight.
steps: Pre-block neurovascular exam: light touch or cold in the target territory and motor function, against the other side.
Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry on, lipid emulsion confirmed, before any injection.
Prep the lateral neck.
Probe transverse in the supraclavicular fossa: find the subclavian artery and plexus ('bunch of grapes').
Trace the plexus cephalad to the 'stoplight' sign between the anterior and middle scalenes.
Insert the needle in-plane, posterior to anterior (lateral to medial).
Advance through the middle scalene until the tip is in the interscalene groove.
Aspirate, then inject 1-2 mL to confirm spread (hydrodissection).
Inject the rest in 3-5 mL aliquots around C5-C7, aspirating between each.
Withdraw and apply a sterile dressing.
ultrasound: SCM superficial; carotid artery medial.
Anterior scalene deep to the SCM and lateral to the internal jugular vein; middle scalene lateral to it.
'Stoplight' sign: C5, C6, C7 roots as three stacked hypoechoic circles in the fascial plane between the scalenes.
confirmation: Anechoic spread around the C5-C7 roots in the interscalene groove.
Sensory loss over the shoulder/deltoid.
Weak shoulder abduction (deltoid) and elbow flexion (biceps).
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Needle hard to see: adjust the angle of incidence, heel-toe, or jiggle the needle.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting - possible intraneural injection. Withdraw 1-2 mm and reposition. Never push harder.
Symptomatic phrenic palsy: sit up, give oxygen, monitor saturation and work of breathing. Escalate if saturation falls below baseline, work of breathing rises, or they cannot speak in full sentences.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
complications: Phrenic nerve palsy (hemidiaphragmatic paresis) - volume-dependent, not universal
Intravascular injection (vertebral or carotid artery) causing LAST
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Dorsal scapular or long thoracic nerve injury
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor at least 30 minutes for LAST.
Sling the arm to prevent traction injury.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Indication and consent (written or verbal per policy).
Spread in the interscalene groove on ultrasound.
No vascular puncture, intraneural injection, or other immediate complications.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
seniorPearls: Tracing up from the supraclavicular fossa is often easier than starting at the neck.
Surrounding every root is unnecessary; the fascial plane usually suffices.
Assume the phrenic nerve will be blocked; never block bilaterally.
The path crosses the middle scalene and its dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves: keep the tip in view, do not advance to a remembered depth.
references: Riazi S, et al. Effect of local anaesthetic volume (20 vs 5 mL) on the efficacy and respiratory consequences of ultrasound-guided interscalene brachial plexus block. Br J Anaesth. 2008;101(4):549-556. https://doi.org/10.1093/bja/aen229 — Found hemidiaphragmatic paresis in 100% of patients at 20 mL versus 45% at 5 mL, demonstrating a volume-dependent effect.
ACEP Sonoguide. Interscalene Nerve Block. https://www.acep.org/sonoguide/nerve-blocks/interscalene-nerve-block
ASRA Pain Medicine. Consensus practice infection control guidelines for regional anesthesia and pain medicine. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2025. https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2024-105651

Neal JM, et al. The Third American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine Practice Advisory on Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2018;43(2):113-123. https://doi.org/10.1097/AAP.0000000000000720

ASRA Pain Medicine. Checklist for Treatment of Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity. 2020. https://www.asra.com/guidelines-articles/original-articles/article-item/asra-news/2020/11/01/checklist-for-treatment-of-local-anesthetic-systemic-toxicity
ASRA Pain Medicine. Regional anesthesia in the patient receiving antithrombotic or thrombolytic therapy, fifth edition. Reg Anesth Pain Med. 2025. https://doi.org/10.1136/rapm-2024-105766
FDA/DailyMed. Bupivacaine hydrochloride injection prescribing information. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/fda/fdaDrugXsl.cfm?setid=02d0e5f1-5fab-4420-b673-785fd81d7ae2&type=display
FDA/DailyMed. Ropivacaine hydrochloride injection prescribing information. https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=8c5c762f-d266-4b1a-809e-f11bfc89bc2d
Verify local anaesthetic policy, antithrombotic policy, and credentialing expectations for this block where you work.

legend.label: Shoulder and lateral upper arm, and the radial side of the forearm to the wrist; the shoulder joint, the humerus and the lateral clavicle.
The cape of the shoulder and the skin over the clavicle, from spread of the same injection.

visualAssets.subtitle: Supine or semi-recumbent, head turned slightly away. Linear probe transverse over the supraclavicular fossa, then trace the plexus cephalad to the interscalene level. Needle in-plane from posterior to anterior (lateral to medial), through the middle scalene.

shiftMode: Covers the arm from the distal humerus: elbow, forearm, wrist, and hand.
Target: brachial plexus trunks/divisions ('bunch of grapes') lateral and superficial to the subclavian artery.
Pneumothorax risk: the pleura is just deep to the artery. Keep the tip in view.
Keep the first rib in view as the backstop between needle and pleura.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Fractures of the distal humerus, elbow, forearm, wrist, or hand
Complex lacerations or amputations of the upper extremity
Painful procedures involving the arm below the mid-humerus
contraindications: Severe baseline pulmonary disease (phrenic palsy or pneumothorax risk)
Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy: deep block - ASRA applies neuraxial-equivalent timing. Use the drug-specific interval from local policy.
anatomy: The subclavian artery rests on the first rib.
The pleura lies immediately deep to the first rib and medial to the artery.
'Corner pocket': deep to the plexus, superficial to the first rib, lateral to the artery.
equipment: High-frequency linear transducer
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle: echogenic, short bevel, e.g., 21G or 22G, 50mm
Local anesthetic: 20 mL total of 0.25% or 0.5% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine.
Normal saline for hydrodissection
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located.
positioning: Supine or semi-recumbent, head turned slightly away.
Arm at the side or across the abdomen.
steps: Pre-block neurovascular exam: light touch or cold in the target territory and motor function, against the other side.
Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry on, lipid emulsion confirmed, before any injection.
Prep the supraclavicular fossa.
Probe transverse in the supraclavicular fossa, aimed caudally: subclavian artery, first rib, pleura, and the plexus lateral to the artery.
Insert the needle in-plane, lateral to medial, aiming for the corner pocket.
Aspirate, then inject 1-2 mL of saline to confirm position.
Inject 15 mL in the corner pocket.
Withdraw slightly and redirect to the superficial plexus for the remaining 5 mL.
Remove the needle and apply a dressing.
ultrasound: Subclavian artery: large, pulsatile, anechoic circle.
First rib: hyperechoic line with posterior acoustic shadowing just deep to the artery.
Pleura: hyperechoic line medial to the rib, with lung sliding.
Brachial plexus: hypoechoic honeycomb ('bunch of grapes') lateral/superficial to the artery.
confirmation: Anechoic spread around the plexus, expanding the corner pocket.
Sensory and motor loss below the mid-humerus.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: First rib not visible: do not advance. The pleura is directly underneath.
Needle tip lost: stop and hydrodissect with saline to find it. Do not advance blindly.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Pneumothorax - the most serious risk (needle too deep or medial)
Phrenic nerve palsy - less common than with interscalene
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor for at least 30 minutes.
Sling the arm to prevent traction injury.
Assess for breathlessness: pneumothorax or phrenic palsy.
Pneumothorax can present hours later: tell the patient to return for new breathlessness or pleuritic pain, and hand that over.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent and indication.
Spread in the corner pocket and around the plexus on ultrasound.
First rib visualized and pleura avoided.
No vascular puncture or intraneural injection.

seniorPearls: Aim for the first rib: hitting it means you are clear of the pleura. Then slide up into the corner pocket.
Injecting the corner pocket first floats the plexus up, making the rest easier and safer.

shiftMode: Retroclavicular Approach to the Infraclavicular Region (RAPTIR).
Forearm and hand trauma.
Less phrenic and pleural risk than a supraclavicular block, but not zero.
The needle crosses the clavicle's acoustic shadow, where the tip can't be seen.
Target: axillary artery posterior to pectoralis minor; the cords surround it.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Fractures of the forearm, wrist, or hand
Complex lacerations or amputations below the elbow
Phrenic palsy or pneumothorax would be poorly tolerated - lower risk, not risk-free
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Patient refusal, inability to cooperate, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Local anesthetic allergy
Coagulopathy (site less compressible)
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy: deep block - ASRA applies neuraxial-equivalent timing. Use the drug-specific interval from local antithrombotic policy.
anatomy: The cords (lateral, posterior, medial) surround the axillary artery deep to pectoralis major and minor.
equipment: High-frequency linear or curvilinear transducer, by depth
Sterile ultrasound gel and probe cover
Sterile gloves
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Regional block needle: echogenic, longer, e.g., 21G 80-100mm
Local anesthetic, standard volume: 20-30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine (30 mL = 75 mg) or 0.2% ropivacaine (30 mL = 60 mg)
Local anesthetic at 0.5%: cap the volume at 20 mL (= 100 mg) and confirm the total against the weight-based maximum before drawing up
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located.
positioning: Supine, head neutral or turned slightly away.
Arm adducted, resting on the abdomen.
steps: Pre-block neurovascular exam: light touch or cold in the target territory and motor function, against the other side.
Cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry on, lipid emulsion confirmed, before any injection.
Transducer sagittal over the infraclavicular fossa: axillary artery and vein deep to the pectoralis muscles.
Prep the skin posterior to the clavicle.
Insert the needle posterior to the clavicle, aiming caudally, strictly in-plane.
Advance under the clavicle until the tip enters the beam in the infraclavicular space.
Tip not back in view past the clavicle: withdraw, don't explore.
Aim for the posterior aspect of the axillary artery (about 6 o'clock).
Aspirate and inject a small saline test dose.
Inject 20-30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine or 0.2% ropivacaine for a U-shaped spread around the artery.
Withdraw the needle and apply a dressing.
ultrasound: Pectoralis major superficial, pectoralis minor deep.
Axillary artery: pulsatile anechoic circle deep to the muscles.
Axillary vein usually medial/caudal to the artery.
Cords: hyperechoic dots around the artery.
confirmation: Anechoic U-shaped or circumferential spread around the axillary artery.
Sensory and motor loss below the elbow.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Trajectory unclear: withdraw and redirect. A probe too close to the clavicle obstructs the view.
Vein in the way: adjust the angle or ease probe pressure so it is not compressed out of view.
Spread on one side of the artery only: consider a second injection; large volumes often spread enough.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
Breathlessness, chest pain, or falling saturation: think pneumothorax and hemothorax, scan the chest, escalate. This site does not compress.
complications: Vascular puncture (axillary artery/vein): hematoma or LAST
Peripheral nerve injury, usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
aftercare: Monitor for at least 30 minutes.
Sling the arm to prevent traction injury.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent and indication.
Spread around the axillary artery on ultrasound.
No vascular puncture.

shiftMode: Target: radial nerve in the proximal forearm, lateral to the radial artery.
Covers the dorsal thumb, index, and lateral middle finger.
Block as proximally as artery and nerve stay in view together.
Combine with median and ulnar for complete hand anesthesia.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Lacerations or fractures of the dorsal hand (radial aspect)
Procedures on the thumb or index finger (dorsal)
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy (relative)
anatomy: Proximal forearm: the radial nerve runs deep to brachioradialis, giving off articular branches.
Mid-forearm: on the lateral side of the radial artery, in the same fascial plane.

equipment: High-frequency linear transducer
25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)

Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and sterile gel.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is.
positioning: Arm supinated and extended.
steps: Probe transverse on the volar forearm; slide laterally to the radial artery.
Find the hyperechoic radial nerve directly lateral to the artery; slide proximally as far as both stay in view.
Insert the needle in-plane.
Aspirate, then inject 5-7 mL around the nerve.
Confirm circumferential spread around the nerve before withdrawing.

confirmation: Numbness in the radial nerve distribution.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.

Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site

caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting - do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

Bilateral truncal fascial-plane blocks are where the ceiling is most misleading. Bilateral TAP dosing at 3 mg/kg ropivacaine, and bilateral 200 mg totals, have produced potentially toxic plasma concentrations in published pharmacokinetic studies - at doses a weight-based calculator calls acceptable. Use the concentration and volume on this card, which keep the bilateral total well below that; do not dose up to the calculated maximum.

shiftMode: Target: femoral nerve lateral to the femoral artery, deep to the fascia iliaca.
Anesthetizes the anterior thigh, femur, and knee.
NAVEL, lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Femur fractures (mid-shaft)
Patellar fractures or severe knee trauma
Large lacerations on the anterior thigh
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Prior femoral vascular surgery or graft at the injection site
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Therapeutic anticoagulation or significant coagulopathy: relative - weigh risk/benefit and local policy.
anatomy: The femoral nerve lies lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle, just distal to the inguinal ligament, under the fascia iliaca.
equipment: High-frequency linear transducer
Regional block needle (21G or 22G, 50-100mm)
Local anesthetic (15-20 mL of 0.25% or 0.5% bupivacaine)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and gel.
Oxygen, suction, airway kit, and resuscitation equipment in the room.
20% lipid emulsion located.
positioning: Supine, leg extended.
steps: Place the transducer transversely over the femoral crease.
Identify the femoral artery and vein, and the femoral nerve lateral to the artery.
Insert the needle in-plane, lateral to medial.
Advance until the tip pops through the fascia iliaca beside the nerve.
Aspirate, then inject 15-20 mL.
ultrasound: Nerve: hyperechoic, often triangular or oval cluster lateral to the pulsatile artery.
confirmation: Anechoic fluid around the nerve beneath the fascia iliaca.
Loss of anterior thigh sensation and weak knee extension (quadriceps).
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Test the target territory before blocking: light touch or cold, and motor function where present, against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Nerve hard to distinguish from fat or connective tissue: tilt the probe to use anisotropy.
Spread superficial to the fascia iliaca: withdraw slightly and redirect deeper.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
aftercare: Expect significant quadriceps weakness and a high fall risk: strict non-weight-bearing until the block wears off. Tell the patient and say so at handover.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Compartment syndrome still shows through a working block: rising analgesic requirement, or pain breaking through.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Consent; spread below the fascia iliaca confirmed; fall-risk warning given.
Side and level, named unambiguously.
Agent, concentration, volume, and the total in milligrams. Any local anesthetic already given this encounter, and the running total.
Needle type and gauge, approach, and whether ultrasound guidance was in-plane or out-of-plane.
Aspiration before each increment; dose given incrementally, not as one push.
Neurological examination before and after the block, with any pre-existing deficit recorded as pre-existing.
Bleeding-risk assessment and its conclusion, including any antithrombotic the patient is taking.
Whether the block worked; if not, what was done instead and how much of the ceiling it used.
seniorPearls: Dense quadriceps weakness: document that the patient was told they cannot walk on that leg.

anatomy: Supraorbital notch/foramen: superior orbital rim, usually in line with the pupil in neutral gaze.
The supratrochlear nerve exits slightly medial to it.
equipment: 25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
1% or 2% lidocaine with epinephrine, 4 mL total.

positioning: Supine or seated.
steps: Palpate the supraorbital notch on the superior orbital rim.
Prep the skin.
Insert subcutaneously just above the eyebrow, aiming medially over the notch.
Aspirate, then inject 2 mL subcutaneously over the notch.
Stay subcutaneous at the rim; do not seek or enter the notch or foramen.
Supratrochlear: advance medially toward the nasal bridge in the same plane and inject 2 mL.
Keep a finger or gauze along the orbital rim below the needle throughout; never direct or advance the needle into the orbit.
Stop for pain or paresthesia.
ultrasound: Not typically required. Can identify the notch (a break in the hyperechoic orbital rim) when swelling obscures landmarks.
confirmation: Numbness of the forehead and anterior scalp back to the vertex.
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Test the target territory before blocking: light touch or cold, and motor function where present, against the other side.

troubleshooting: Partial block: wait out the onset time, then supplement rather than repeat.

Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site; black eye if it tracks into the eyelid
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
aftercare: Warn about eyelid swelling if the volume was large.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Return if numbness or weakness outlasts expectation, pain is new or escalating, or the site reddens.

steps: **Intraoral approach:**
Palpate the infraorbital foramen extraorally with the non-dominant index finger.
Topical anesthetic to the buccal mucosa above the maxillary canine/first premolar.
Retract the upper lip.
Insert into the mucobuccal fold above the canine/first premolar, directed superiorly toward the palpating finger.
Stop before hitting bone or entering the foramen.
Aspirate, then inject 2-3 mL.
Keep the palpating finger over the foramen for the whole injection as the stop for the needle.
Advance parallel to the long axis of the first premolar toward the fingertip, about 1.5-2 cm in an adult, then stop.
A shallower angle points at the orbit.
Never advance toward or into the orbit, or past the palpating finger.
Stop for pain, paresthesia, or unexpected resistance.

Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent; more likely if injected into the foramen

0.2% gives analgesia with less motor block and is preferred for fascial plane and continuous blocks; 0.5% for a denser block. Epinephrine is not needed - ropivacaine causes less vasodilation than lidocaine or bupivacaine, so it is absorbed more slowly. dosing.cumulativeWarning: Maximums are not interchangeable - two agents do not share one number of milligrams. Work each agent out as a fraction of its own ceiling; the fractions must add to less than one. Count everything: skin wheals, wound infiltration, any earlier block this encounter, and both sides of a bilateral block.
monitoring: Weigh or estimate the patient and calculate the maximum in mg AND mL before drawing up - say it out loud.
Continuous cardiac monitoring and pulse oximetry from before injection through at least 30 minutes after.
Confirm where 20% lipid emulsion is stocked before injecting - do not start without a LAST plan.
Aspirate before injecting and give the dose in 3 mL increments with repeat aspiration.
caveats: Use lean body weight in obese patients.
Reduce by about 25% at the extremes of age or with severe comorbidity.

The same milligram dose peaks higher from a vascular bed - intercostal, mucosal, a truncal fascial plane, an inflamed field - than from a subcutaneous wheal, so the ceiling is a limit rather than a target.

These ceilings are this app's governed policy, set by the clinical owner. The drug labels publish no universal figure per agent - they require individualization by block, site, patient size, and physical status. Staying under the number is necessary, not sufficient.

shiftMode: Target: ring block at the base of the ear for the greater auricular, lesser occipital, and auriculotemporal nerves.
Anesthetizes the auricle except the external auditory canal and concha.
No epinephrine - cartilage ischemia risk.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Complex ear lacerations
Auricular hematoma drainage
contraindications: Infection over the injection site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy (relative)
anatomy: Several nerves reach the ear from different directions.
A diamond-shaped subcutaneous ring around the base of the ear blocks them all.
equipment: 25G or 27G needle (1.5 inch)
Local anesthetic (5-10 mL of 1% lidocaine or 0.5% bupivacaine, without epinephrine)
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Sterile gloves; single-use sterile probe cover and gel for ultrasound.
Know where the 20% lipid emulsion is before injecting.
positioning: Seated, or lateral decubitus with the affected ear up.
steps: Prep the skin around the entire ear.
Insert just inferior to the earlobe; inject subcutaneously, tracking anteriorly in front of the tragus.
From the same puncture, track posteriorly behind the earlobe along the mastoid, injecting subcutaneously.
Insert just superior to the ear; track anteriorly to meet the first track.
From the superior puncture, track posteriorly to meet the second track, completing the ring.
ultrasound: Not used.
confirmation: Complete numbness of the auricle (pinna).
Spread on the screen shows where the drug went.
Test the target territory before blocking: light touch or cold, and motor function where present, against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Concha still painful: vagal/facial innervation from deeper - a local wheal in the concha may be needed.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Cartilage necrosis (with epinephrine; controversial, best avoided)
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Bleeding or hematoma at the injection site
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
aftercare: Routine wound care, or compression dressing for hematomas.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Return if numbness or weakness outlasts expectation, pain is new or escalating, or the site reddens.
documentation: No epinephrine used.

seniorPearls: Use a long needle: two punctures (inferior and superior) complete the ring.

shiftMode: Target: greater occipital nerve at the superior nuchal line, just medial to the occipital artery.
Migraine in the ED: bilateral, 3 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine a side.
Rule out a secondary headache first.
Calculate the max dose (mg and mL) before drawing up - say it out loud.
Aspirate before each increment and inject in stages.
Decide the backup plan before you start.
indications: Acute migraine in the ED, after or alongside first-line parenteral treatment
Occipital neuralgia
Tension-type headache (limited evidence)
contraindications: Suspected secondary headache, a focal neurological deficit, or headache after head trauma: work it up first
Infection over the injection site
Open skull defect at the site
Allergy to local anesthetic
Patient refusal, or inability to consent where the block is not time-critical
Pre-existing neurological deficit in the target territory - document before blocking.
Antithrombotic therapy (relative)
anatomy: The greater occipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C2. It ascends between obliquus capitis inferior and semispinalis capitis and reaches the scalp at the superior nuchal line.

At the superior nuchal line it lies about one-third of the way from the external occipital protuberance to the mastoid, about 2 cm lateral to the protuberance, just medial to the occipital artery. The position varies.
The lesser occipital, third occipital and greater auricular nerves lie nearby.
equipment: 23G or 25G needle, 1-1.5 inch
0.5% bupivacaine, 3 mL a side (6 mL for a bilateral block), or 2% lidocaine.
Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin prep, left to dry.
Gauze.
20% lipid emulsion located.
positioning: Seated with the neck flexed forward, or prone.
steps: Palpate the external occipital protuberance and the mastoid process.
Mark the point one-third of the way from the protuberance to the mastoid, on the superior nuchal line.
Feel for the occipital artery there; the entry point is just medial to it. The point of maximal tenderness can confirm it.
Part the hair (no need to shave) and prep the skin.
Insert perpendicular to the skin until resistance, withdraw 1 mm, and aspirate.
Inject 3 mL: 1 mL at the point, 1 mL medial, 1 mL lateral, aspirating before each.
For migraine, repeat on the other side.
ultrasound: Not required for the landmark technique. Color Doppler can locate the occipital artery when it cannot be felt.
confirmation: Numbness of the back of the scalp from the occiput toward the vertex.
Reassess the headache at 30 minutes.
Test the target territory before blocking: light touch or cold, and motor function where present, against the other side.
Give the agent its onset time before judging: lidocaine 5-10 minutes, bupivacaine and ropivacaine 15-30.
troubleshooting: Blood on aspiration: withdraw, hold pressure, and redirect medially, away from the artery.
Lightheaded or faint: lay the patient flat.
Partial block: wait out the full onset time, then supplement rather than repeat. Check the remaining allowance on the calculator before drawing up more.
Failed block: do not re-inject the same volume in the same place. Options are a different level, a block of the overlapping nerve, infiltration within the remaining ceiling, or systemic analgesia.
Pain on injection, paresthesia, or high resistance: stop injecting and reposition. Never push harder.
complications: Bleeding, pain or swelling at the injection site
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity - see the linked rescue card
Nerve injury - usually transient, occasionally permanent
aftercare: Observe for dizziness or vasovagal symptoms before discharge.
Protect the insensate part: pad it, position it, and warn the patient about pressure and heat while the block lasts.
Tell the patient when the block will wear off and to take oral analgesia before it does.
Return precautions: numbness or weakness lasting longer than expected, new or escalating pain, or redness at the injection site.
documentation: Headache score before the block and at 30 minutes.

seniorPearls: With 3 mL, spread to the lesser occipital nerve is possible.
Steroid adds nothing for migraine over local anesthetic alone, and brings alopecia and skin atrophy at the site.
